research.domain: XRPL developer client libraries, signing/codec primitives, wallet & faucet helpers, and EVM-sidechain dev stack
research.notes: 2026 synthesis: For JS/TS apps (web + Node) use xrpl.js (v5.0.0) — it is the de-facto reference SDK and bundles the codec/keypair primitives, a Wallet class, and a fundWallet faucet helper. For Python backends, ML/data tooling, and scripting use xrpl-py (v5.0.0) — feature-parity with xrpl.js and the cleanest typed-model API. For JVM/enterprise (Java, Kotlin, Android) use xrpl4j (v6.0.0 stable; 6.1.0-rc.1 in flight) — immutable Immutables-generated models, JDK 1.8+. The low-level primitives (ripple-binary-codec v2.8.0, ripple-keypairs v3.0.0, ripple-address-codec v5.0.1) are normally consumed transitively via xrpl.js — only pull them directly for custom signers, offline cold-signing, or codec/interop tooling. Note the 5.0 line of xrpl.js AND xrpl-py both shipped a BREAKING change to the default signing algorithm (now inferred from seed prefix / ed25519-leaning) in June 2026 — pin versions and read migration notes. For smart contracts use the XRPL EVM sidechain (mainnet live since 2025-06-30, chain ID 1440000, native gas = XRP) with standard ethers.js / web3.js / viem against its Ethereum JSON-RPC — the native XRPL SDKs do NOT talk to the EVM sidechain.

capabilities.name: xrpl.js
capabilities.summary: The official JavaScript/TypeScript SDK for the XRP Ledger, maintained by XRPLF. Current major version is 5.0.0 (published 2026-06-05). It works in both Node.js and the browser, providing a Client class for WebSocket/JSON-RPC network calls, a Wallet class for key management/signing, transaction autofill/submit-and-wait helpers, and a built-in faucet helper (fundWallet). It is the most complete and most-documented XRPL client and the default choice for any JS/TS stack.

key_fields.key_apis: Client (connect, request, submitAndWait, fundWallet), Wallet (generate, fromSeed, fromSecret, sign), autofill, getBalances, dropsToXrp/xrpToDrops, subscribe streams

capabilities.gotchas: v5.0.0 is a BREAKING release: it changed the default choice of signing algorithm and now infers the algorithm from the seed prefix in Wallet.fromSeed/fromSecret, and throws on server_info failure or missing network_id. Pin your version and re-test signing/address derivation when upgrading from 4.x. Browser builds may need polyfills for some Node globals (see UNIQUE_SETUPS.md). The faucet/fundWallet helper only works on public test networks (testnet/devnet), not mainnet.

best_for.purpose: Web/Node app integration with XRPL
Minting and trading NFTs (NFTokens)
In-game token/economy plumbing in a JS/TS client
Issuing credentials / compliance flows from a TS backend

capabilities.name: xrpl-py
capabilities.summary: The official Python SDK for the XRP Ledger, maintained by XRPLF. Current major version is 5.0.0 (released 2026-06-03), requiring Python 3.10+. It offers typed transaction/request models, sync and asyncio JSON-RPC/WebSocket clients, a Wallet abstraction, codec/keypair primitives, and faucet helpers. It is the go-to for Python backends, data/ML tooling, bots, and scripting, with feature parity to xrpl.js.

Python 3.8 and 3.9 support was dropped; you must be on 3.10+. ConfidentialMPT support that first appeared in a 4.6.0b0 beta is folded into newer releases — confirm amendment availability on your target network before using bleeding-edge transaction types.

capabilities.name: xrpl4j
capabilities.summary: The official 100% Java SDK for the XRP Ledger, maintained by XRPLF. Current stable major version is 6.0.0 (released 2026-01-13), with 6.1.0-rc.1 a release candidate in progress. It targets JDK 1.8+ and is organized into modules — xrpl4j-core (seeds, keys for secp256k1/ed25519, address & binary codecs, immutable transaction/request models) and xrpl4j-client (a JSON-RPC client for rippled). It is the default choice for JVM, Kotlin, and Android backends.

The library leans on Immutables-generated builders, so model construction is verbose compared to xrpl.js/xrpl-py. Pull artifacts together via the BOM to avoid mismatched module versions.

capabilities.name: ripple-binary-codec
capabilities.summary: The low-level (de)serialization library that encodes/decodes XRPL transactions and ledger objects to and from the canonical binary format used for signing and the wire protocol. Current major version is 2.8.0 (published 2026-06-05) within the xrpl.js monorepo. Most builders consume it transitively through xrpl.js; pull it directly only for custom signers, offline/cold-signing tooling, or binary interop.
capabilities.gotchas: This is a primitive, not a full client — it does no network I/O and no key management. Its definitions.json must match the field/type definitions of the rippled version and amendments you target; using a stale codec against a network with new fields can produce encode/decode errors. Prefer using it via xrpl.js unless you specifically need raw binary control.

best_for.purpose: Custom or offline transaction signing
Binary interop / ledger-object decoding tools

capabilities.name: ripple-keypairs
capabilities.summary: The cryptographic keypair and signing primitive for XRPL, supporting both secp256k1 and ed25519. Current major version is 3.0.0 (published 2026-06-05) within the xrpl.js monorepo. It generates seeds, derives keypairs and classic addresses, and signs/verifies arbitrary messages. Builders normally use it via the xrpl.js Wallet class; use it directly for custom key handling, HSM integration, or bespoke signers.
capabilities.gotchas: Default-algorithm behavior shifted across the 2026 monorepo release (xrpl.js 5.0 infers algorithm from seed prefix) — be explicit about secp256k1 vs ed25519 when deriving keypairs to avoid generating the wrong address from a given seed. This is signing only; it does no network I/O. Handle seeds/secrets as sensitive material and never log them.

best_for.purpose: Custom signers and HSM/key-management integration

capabilities.name: ripple-address-codec
capabilities.summary: The encoder/decoder for XRPL addresses, seeds, and node keys, including classic (base58) addresses and X-addresses (which embed a destination tag). Current version is 5.0.1 (published 2026-06-04) within the xrpl.js monorepo. It is the canonical place for classic-address <-> X-address conversion and is consumed transitively by xrpl.js; pull it directly when you only need address validation/conversion.

key_fields.key_apis: classicAddressToXAddress, xAddressToClassicAddress, isValidClassicAddress, isValidXAddress, encodeSeed, decodeSeed

capabilities.gotchas: X-addresses encode the destination tag; converting carelessly between classic address + tag and X-address can drop or mismatch the tag, which on exchanges means lost/misrouted funds. Always validate addresses with isValidClassicAddress/isValidXAddress before use. This is a codec only — no network calls.

capabilities.name: XRPL Wallet & seed handling (Wallet class)
capabilities.summary: The wallet/seed abstraction exposed by the official SDKs (Wallet in xrpl.js and xrpl-py, Seed/KeyPair in xrpl4j) that turns a seed/secret into a signing identity: it holds the keypair, derives the classic address, and signs transactions. As of the 2026 5.0 releases the default signing algorithm is inferred from the seed prefix (ed25519 seeds start with sEd; secp256k1 otherwise), a breaking change builders must understand to derive the correct address.

key_fields.install: Provided by xrpl.js / xrpl-py / xrpl4j (no separate package)

key_fields.secret_formats: family seed (s...), ed25519 seed (sEd...), mnemonic/secret-numbers (separate helpers)

capabilities.gotchas: Breaking in the 5.0 line: the default algorithm is now seed-prefix-inferred — a seed previously decoded as secp256k1 by default may now derive a different address if you don't pass the algorithm explicitly. Never hard-code or commit seeds/secrets; treat them like private keys. The fundWallet/generate_faucet_wallet flow only applies to test networks. For high-value or regulated use, prefer external signing/HSM over in-process seeds.

capabilities.name: Faucet / test-network helpers (fundWallet)
capabilities.summary: Built-in helpers in the official SDKs that auto-fund a wallet with test XRP on public test networks. In xrpl.js, Client.fundWallet() creates or funds a wallet (typically ~1000 XRP) and auto-detects the correct faucet server for testnet/devnet/AMM-devnet/Hooks testnet; xrpl-py exposes generate_faucet_wallet(). They make spinning up a working dev account a one-liner, with custom faucet host/path options for non-default networks.
capabilities.gotchas: Faucets are test-only — there is NO mainnet faucet; calling fundWallet against a mainnet client will fail. Faucets are rate-limited and best-effort, so do not rely on them in CI loops without backoff. On custom/non-standard networks you must pass faucetHost/faucetPath explicitly because auto-detection only covers the well-known public networks.

capabilities.name: xrpl-secret-numbers
capabilities.summary: A helper library for the XRPL 'secret numbers' format — a human-friendlier representation of a seed as eight groups of six digits, designed to reduce transcription errors when backing up an account. Current version is 3.0.0 (published 2026-06-05) within the xrpl.js monorepo. It converts between secret-number strings and the underlying entropy/seed used by the keypair libraries.

key_fields.key_apis: Account class (from secret numbers / from entropy), getSecret, getAddress, getKeypair

capabilities.gotchas: Niche format — most flows use family seeds (s...) directly; only adopt secret numbers if your UX specifically needs the digit-group backup format. The checksum digit on each group catches typos but does not protect against full-group loss. As with all seed material, the resulting secret must be handled as a private key.

best_for.purpose: Human-friendly seed backup/recovery UX

capabilities.name: XRPL EVM sidechain dev stack (ethers / web3 / viem)
capabilities.summary: The XRPL EVM sidechain is an Ethereum-compatible chain (Cosmos SDK + CometBFT, Proof-of-Authority) whose mainnet went live 2025-06-30, using XRP as the native gas token. Because it exposes a standard Ethereum JSON-RPC, you build on it with the normal Ethereum toolchain — ethers.js, web3.js, viem, Hardhat/Foundry, MetaMask — NOT the native XRPL SDKs. Mainnet chain ID is 1440000 (native currency XRP); the testnet is a separate chain ID. Use this when you need Solidity smart contracts alongside XRP.

key_fields.install: npm i ethers (or web3 / viem) — point the provider at the XRPL EVM RPC
key_fields.current_version: Use current ethers v6.x / web3.js v4.x / viem; XRPL EVM mainnet live since 2025-06-30
key_fields.key_apis: Standard EVM JSON-RPC: eth_chainId, eth_sendRawTransaction, eth_call; ethers JsonRpcProvider / Wallet / Contract

capabilities.gotchas: Two different worlds: the native XRPL SDKs (xrpl.js, xrpl-py, xrpl4j) do NOT talk to the EVM sidechain and vice versa — moving value between the XRP Ledger mainnet and the EVM sidechain requires the bridge, not a same-account transfer. Use the correct chain ID — mainnet is 1440000, testnet uses a different ID (chainlist shows 1449000 for a testnet); pointing a wallet at the wrong chain causes failed/duplicated tx. Gas is paid in XRP. Confirm the live RPC endpoint from official docs as endpoints can change.

best_for.purpose: Solidity smart contracts with XRP as gas
EVM NFT/DeFi contracts settling against XRPL ecosystem
Programmable payments / escrow logic in Solidity
On-chain identity/compliance contracts

research.domain: On-chain trading: native CLOB order book, XLS-30 Automated Market Maker, pathfinding, cross-currency, and permissioned/institutional venues
research.notes: As of mid-2026 the XRPL has a mature dual-liquidity DEX. The native central-limit order book (CLOB) has existed since genesis (OfferCreate/OfferCancel) and is enhanced by auto-bridging through XRP and a Flow-based payment engine for cross-currency pathfinding. The XLS-30 Automated Market Maker went live on Mainnet 2024-03-22 (AMM amendment) and is integrated with the CLOB: offers and payments are automatically optimized to route through the pool, the order books, or both for the best rate. AMM uses a geometric-mean (weight 0.5 => constant-product) curve, LPTokens, a 0%-1% governable trading fee (AMMVote), and a 24-hour continuous-auction discount slot (AMMBid). A series of fix amendments hardened it: fixAMMOverflowOffer, fixAMMv1_1, fixAMMv1_2 (all enabled), and fixAMMv1_3 (enabled 2025-08-29). AMMClawback (enabled 2025-01-30, rippled 2.3.0) lets issuers of clawback-enabled tokens recover funds from pools and unblocked RLUSD/regulated-token pools; fixAMMClawbackRounding is still open for voting. The biggest 2026 development is the institutional permissioning stack: Permissioned Domains (XLS-80) enabled 2026-02-04 and Permissioned DEX (XLS-81) enabled 2026-02-18, allowing credential-gated order books. IMPORTANT: permissioned offers/payments CANNOT be filled by AMMs (AMMs are open-DEX only); hybrid offers (tfHybrid) can rest in both the permissioned and open order books. Builder guidance: use the AMM for long-tail token liquidity and passive yield, the CLOB for tight institutional/limit-order trading, pathfinding (ripple_path_find/path_find) for cross-currency UX, and permissioned DEX only for compliance-gated venues.

capabilities.name: OfferCreate (native order-book DEX)
capabilities.summary: Places an offer to trade two assets in the native central-limit order book (CLOB). TakerGets is what you sell, TakerPays is what you want; offers that cross existing offers execute immediately and any remainder rests in the book as an Offer ledger entry. This is the foundational primitive of the XRPL DEX and predates the AMM by over a decade.
capabilities.key_fields: TakerGets (sell amount), TakerPays (buy amount), Expiration (optional, seconds since Ripple Epoch), OfferSequence (cancel prior offer), DomainID (permissioned DEX, optional); flags tfPassive, tfImmediateOrCancel, tfFillOrKill, tfSell, tfHybrid
capabilities.gotchas: Resting offers consume owner reserve (2 XRP/object as of current reserve). Unfunded offers (owner no longer holds TakerGets, unless they issue it) are skipped/auto-removed. Offers with frozen tokens fail. Partial fills still return tesSUCCESS - check metadata for actual amounts. tfSell exchanges the full TakerGets even if you get more than TakerPays.

best_for.purpose: Limit orders and tight spread trading
In-game currency/token markets with price control
Listing in-game items priced in IOUs

capabilities.name: OfferCancel
capabilities.summary: Removes an existing resting Offer from the order books by sequence number, freeing the associated owner reserve. Cancelling a non-existent offer succeeds harmlessly (tesSUCCESS), which simplifies idempotent client logic.
capabilities.key_fields: OfferSequence (the Sequence of the OfferCreate transaction that created the offer to cancel)
capabilities.gotchas: OfferCancel referencing a missing or already-consumed offer still returns tesSUCCESS - do not treat success as proof the offer existed. To atomically replace an offer, prefer OfferCreate with OfferSequence rather than a separate OfferCancel.

best_for.purpose: Order management / canceling stale limit orders
Marketplace listing withdrawal

capabilities.name: Auto-Bridging (XRP as bridge currency)
capabilities.summary: When two non-XRP currencies have thin direct liquidity, offer crossing automatically routes a synthetic trade through XRP (buy XRP with currency A, sell XRP for currency B) if that yields a better composite rate. It happens automatically on OfferCreate offer crossing, deepening effective liquidity across the long tail of token pairs without any extra action by the trader.
capabilities.key_fields: No extra fields - applied automatically during offer crossing; relies on liquidity in both currency/XRP order books
capabilities.gotchas: Auto-bridging applies to offer crossing (OfferCreate), NOT to standard Payment transactions by default - cross-currency payments achieve similar effects through pathfinding instead. Benefit depends on XRP-pair depth; if either XRP book is shallow the synthetic route may not win.

best_for.purpose: Deeper effective liquidity for exotic token pairs

capabilities.name: Pathfinding & Cross-Currency Payments (Flow engine)
capabilities.summary: Cross-currency payments traverse paths of rippling (same-currency through an intermediary) and trading (through order books or AMMs) steps, computed by the Flow payment engine. The ripple_path_find (one-shot) and path_find (WebSocket, updating) methods discover viable paths; default paths cover the common cases and the engine consults both CLOB and AMM liquidity at execution time.
capabilities.key_fields: Payment fields: Amount (destination), SendMax (source cap), DeliverMin (partial-payment floor), Paths; flags tfPartialPayment, tfNoDirectRipple, tfLimitQuality; API methods ripple_path_find, path_find
capabilities.gotchas: rippled is explicitly NOT designed to find the absolute best path - it finds a good one. Paths can become invalid between submission and validation (re-pathfind for high-value sends). tfPartialPayment changes Amount semantics to a maximum - always set DeliverMin and check delivered_amount in metadata to avoid partial-payment exploits.

best_for.purpose: Cross-currency send (user pays in A, recipient gets B)
FX-style settlement across IOUs

capabilities.name: AMM (XLS-30 Automated Market Maker)
capabilities.summary: Native, non-custodial Automated Market Maker integrated directly into the XRPL DEX. It uses a geometric-mean curve with weight 0.5, making it function as a constant-product market maker. Each AMM holds a pool of two assets, issues LPTokens to liquidity providers, and is automatically consulted alongside the order book so offers and payments route through whichever (pool, CLOB, or both) gives the best rate.
capabilities.key_fields: AMM ledger entry holds two pooled Amounts, TradingFee, LPTokenBalance, AuctionSlot, VoteSlots; transactions AMMCreate/Deposit/Withdraw/Vote/Bid/Delete/Clawback; LPToken uses a 160-bit hex currency code derived from a SHA-512 hash of the asset pair
capabilities.gotchas: One AMM per asset pair (duplicates rejected). Both pooled IOUs require Default Ripple enabled on the issuer; LPTokens of another AMM cannot be pooled. Liquidity providers bear impermanent loss. AMM is OPEN-DEX only - it cannot fill permissioned offers/payments. Always seed at the true market ratio; off-ratio pools are immediately arbitraged.

best_for.purpose: Passive liquidity provision / LP yield on token pairs
Bootstrapping liquidity for a new in-game token
Reducing slippage on long-tail tokens

capabilities.name: AMMCreate
capabilities.summary: Creates a new AMM instance for a given asset pair, transferring both seed assets from the sender into a newly created special AMM pseudo-account and issuing initial LPTokens to the creator. It also sets the pool's starting trading fee (0-1000, i.e. 0%-1%).

Double-asset deposits (proportional, fee-free) preserve the pool ratio; single-asset deposits are allowed but incur a fee equivalent to trading part of the deposit for the other asset before a proportional deposit. Flag-driven modes let you target an exact asset amount, an exact LPToken amount, or a price-capped deposit.

capabilities.gotchas: Single-asset deposits cost a slippage-like fee and worsen with size - large single-asset deposits are penalized. Since the AMMClawback amendment, you cannot deposit if either pooled asset is frozen (fails tecFROZEN). tfTwoAssetIfEmpty is the only deposit allowed into a fully-emptied pool (re-seeds ratio).

capabilities.name: AMMVote (governable trading fee)
capabilities.summary: Lets LPToken holders vote on the AMM's trading fee (0-1000 = 0%-1%). The effective fee is the LP-token-weighted average of the latest votes, counting only the top 8 holders by LPToken balance. This decentralizes fee governance to the pool's largest stakeholders.

capabilities.gotchas: Only the 8 largest LP holders' votes count; a small holder's vote is rejected with tecAMM_FAILED_VOTE if 8 larger holders already voted. Voting requires holding the pool's LPTokens (else tecAMM_INVALID_TOKENS). The auction-slot holder's effective fee is 1/10 of the voted fee.

capabilities.name: AMMBid (continuous auction slot)
capabilities.summary: Bids LPTokens to win the AMM's 24-hour auction slot, which grants trading against the pool at 1/10 the normal fee. This is the XLS-30 mechanism that continuously auctions arbitrage advantage and routes the proceeds (burned LPTokens) back to all liquidity providers. Up to 4 additional accounts can be authorized to share the discount.
capabilities.key_fields: Asset, Asset2 (pool), BidMin (floor), BidMax (ceiling), AuthAccounts (up to 4, excluding sender)
capabilities.gotchas: The 24h slot is split into 20 intervals of ~72 min; outbidding refunds the displaced holder R = B*(1-t) (zero in the final interval). You must hold enough LPTokens to cover the bid. Slot timing uses the prior ledger's close time, so expect ~10s variance. Mostly useful to active arbitrageurs/market makers, not casual users.

capabilities.key_fields: Asset, Asset2 (the pool to delete)
capabilities.gotchas: Only works on an already-empty AMM (all LPTokens redeemed). Large pools require multiple AMMDelete calls (512 trust lines per call). research.domain: On-chain identity, KYC/AML, and access-gating primitives on the XRP Ledger
research.notes: As of mid-2026 the XRPL has a near-complete, natively-supported compliance stack live on mainnet. DID (XLS-40) has been live since 31 Oct 2024. Credentials (XLS-70) followed (open for voting in rippled 2.3.0, Nov 2024) and is now enabled — confirmed by the fact that the features that DEPEND on it are live. Permissioned Domains (XLS-80) went live on mainnet 4 Feb 2026 with ~91% validator support, and Permissioned DEXes (which require Credentials + Permissioned Domains) shipped on top. The intended composition for a regulated app/game is: an accredited issuer mints Credentials -> the relying app turns on DepositAuth and adds credential-based DepositPreauth, OR creates a Permissioned Domain whose AcceptedCredentials gate transfers, DEX trading, lending and vaults. DID is the self-sovereign identity anchor; Credentials are the attestations; Permissioned Domains are the enforcement envelope. KEY CAVEAT: none of these put PII on-chain — Credentials store only an issuer attestation + an optional URI to off-ledger data, and DIDs are explicitly warned against holding personal data. Region-gating/KYC is therefore done by trusting an off-chain verifier (the credential issuer), not by the ledger validating identity itself. A separate PermissionDelegation amendment that touched this area was found buggy and was removed in rippled v2.6.1; do not rely on it.

capabilities.name: Decentralized Identifiers (DID)
capabilities.summary: Adds a W3C-conformant Decentralized Identifier (the did:xrpl method) anchored to an XRPL account. The owner controls a DID ledger entry holding an on-ledger minimal DID document, arbitrary Data, or a URI pointing to an off-ledger document (IPFS/STORJ). It is the self-sovereign identity root that Verifiable Credentials and compliance flows reference. Control of the DID equals control of the account's private key.
gotchas: DIDs are fully public — never store PII, KYC documents, or personal data on-ledger; reference content-addressed off-ledger storage (IPFS) instead.
One DID per account (the DID ledger entry is keyed to the account); there is no multi-DID-per-account model.
Implicit DID documents can be derived from the account's public key even with no DIDDocument/URI set, which surprises builders expecting an empty resolve.
DID alone proves no identity — it must be paired with Credentials/Verifiable Credentials from a trusted issuer to mean anything for KYC.

best_for.purpose: Self-sovereign identity anchor for a player/account
Reference target for off-ledger verifiable credentials
DeFi/access-control identity root

capabilities.name: Credentials (on-chain attestations)
capabilities.summary: A W3C-aligned framework for issuing signed, on-ledger attestations about an account (KYC status, accreditation, region eligibility). An issuer mints a Credential to a subject; the subject must accept it for it to become valid. Credentials are the building block that powers credential-based Deposit Authorization, Permissioned Domains, and Permissioned DEXes. It stores only an issuer attestation plus an optional URI — never the underlying PII.
gotchas: A credential is inert until the subject accepts it (CredentialAccept sets lsfAccepted); relying parties must check the accepted flag, not just existence.
Credentials carry no PII — they only attest 'issuer X says subject Y has type Z'; trust is entirely in the off-chain issuer/verifier, so region-gating is only as good as the issuer.
Expiration is enforced at use time: an offer, payment, or domain membership silently becomes invalid once the credential expires.
Revocation is by deletion (CredentialDelete) — there is no on-chain revocation history, so auditing past validity requires off-ledger logging.
CredentialType is opaque arbitrary bytes (max 64); both issuer and relying party must agree on its meaning out-of-band.

best_for.purpose: On-chain KYC/accreditation attestation for regulated access
Region/age gating for a game economy or token sale
Pre-approving verified counterparties for payments

capabilities.name: CredentialCreate / CredentialAccept / CredentialDelete
capabilities.summary: The three-transaction lifecycle of a credential. CredentialCreate (sent by the issuer) mints a credential for a Subject with a CredentialType, optional Expiration, and optional URI. CredentialAccept (sent by the subject) marks it accepted/valid (sets lsfAccepted). CredentialDelete (issuer or subject) removes it, which is also the revocation mechanism.
gotchas: Issuer and Subject may be the same account (self-issued credential) — relying parties should verify the Issuer is a trusted authority, not just that a credential exists.
CredentialType is hex on the wire and capped at 64 bytes; URI is capped at 256 bytes — keep payloads tiny and push real data off-ledger.
Until CredentialAccept runs, the credential exists but is not usable for DepositPreauth or domain membership.
CredentialDelete by the subject is a legitimate self-removal path; issuers cannot prevent a subject from deleting an accepted credential.

best_for.purpose: Mint a KYC attestation to a verified user
User-side acceptance step in an onboarding flow
Revoke a credential when status changes

sources.title: CredentialCreate — xrpl.org transaction reference

capabilities.name: Deposit Authorization (DepositAuth flag)
capabilities.summary: An account flag (asfDepositAuth, value 9 / lsfDepositAuth 0x01000000) that blocks all incoming transfers of XRP and tokens from strangers. Once set, the account can only receive funds from explicitly preauthorized senders, via two-step protocols (Checks, Escrow, Payment Channels), or by self-initiated transactions. It is the foundational on/off switch for a compliant, allow-list-only account.
gotchas: Even with DepositAuth on, an account below its reserve can still receive XRP up to the reserve amount from anyone — not a hard block at low balances.
Rippling and DEX offers create exceptions, so DepositAuth does not stop all token inflows; pair with RequireAuth/freezes for issued assets.
Preauthorization is currency-agnostic — you cannot preauthorize a sender for one currency only.
Two-step protocols (Check/Escrow/PayChan) bypass the stranger block because the destination initiates receipt; account for that in compliance assumptions.

best_for.purpose: Allow-list-only treasury or regulated app account
Block unsolicited dust/spam payments
Custodial/escrow account that only accepts known senders

sources.title: Deposit Authorization — xrpl.org
sources.claim: DepositAuth (asfDepositAuth value 9) blocks all transfers from strangers and only allows preauthorized senders, two-step protocols, or self-initiated transactions; preauthorization is currency-agnostic.

capabilities.name: DepositPreauth (account + credential preauthorization)
capabilities.summary: Grants exceptions to a DepositAuth-enabled account. The transaction takes exactly one of four fields: Authorize / Unauthorize (by specific account address) or AuthorizeCredentials / UnauthorizeCredentials (by a set of {Issuer, CredentialType} pairs, enabled by the Credentials amendment). Credential-based preauth lets any sender holding the right accepted credentials deposit — no per-account allow-listing — which is the scalable KYC gate.
gotchas: Exactly one of the four fields must be present — mixing account and credential authorization in one transaction fails.
Each account-based preauth creates a DepositPreauth ledger object that consumes owner reserve; credential-based preauth scales better because one rule covers all matching holders.
AuthorizeCredentials requires the sender to hold an ACCEPTED credential at deposit time; an unaccepted or expired credential silently fails the deposit.
Cannot preauthorize yourself; preauthorizations are one-directional.

best_for.purpose: Scalable KYC gate — accept any deposit from holders of an approved credential
Explicit per-counterparty allow-list for a custodial account
Region-gated payment acceptance via a region credential

sources.title: DepositPreauth — xrpl.org transaction reference
sources.claim: DepositPreauth takes exactly one of Authorize, Unauthorize, AuthorizeCredentials, or UnauthorizeCredentials; the credential fields take {Issuer, CredentialType} pairs and are enabled by the Credentials amendment.

capabilities.name: Permissioned Domains
capabilities.summary: A managed, rule-based environment within the public ledger where activity is restricted to accounts holding accepted credentials. A domain owner defines AcceptedCredentials (a set of {Issuer, CredentialType}); any account holding a matching accepted credential is a member. Domains are the enforcement envelope that lets banks, exchanges, and regulated games run KYC/AML-gated activity on mainnet, and they are the substrate for Permissioned DEXes, Lending, and Vaults. Went live 4 Feb 2026 with ~91% validator support.
gotchas: Membership is dynamic and evaluated at use time — if a member's credential expires or the domain's AcceptedCredentials change, that account immediately loses access (in-flight offers/positions can become invalid).
Trust is delegated to the domain owner and the credential issuers; the ledger does not verify identity itself, so a compromised or lax issuer compromises the whole domain.
AcceptedCredentials is a set — an account qualifies by holding any one matching accepted credential, so be deliberate about which issuer/type combinations you list.
A maintenance upgrade (fixCleanup3_1_3, ~May 2026) bundled fixes for Permissioned Domains, NFTs, Vaults and Lending — treat the feature as new and stay current on rippled patches.

capabilities.name: RequireAuth (authorized trust lines)
capabilities.summary: An issuer account flag (asfRequireAuth, value 2) that requires the issuer to explicitly authorize each trust line before a holder can receive the issuer's token. It is the classic permissioned-issuance gate: combined with KYC off-chain, an issuer only authorizes trust lines for verified accounts, making the token itself allow-list-only. Must be set before the issuer has any tokens outstanding.
gotchas: RequireAuth can only be enabled while the issuer has zero issued balances/trust lines — you cannot retrofit it onto a live token.
Authorization is per-trust-line and one-way (issuer authorizes holder); it does not gate the holder from sending to third parties once authorized.
It controls who may HOLD the token, which is a different axis from DepositAuth (who may PAY an account) — regulated assets usually need both plus freezes.
Manual authorization does not scale; for large user bases prefer Credential-gated Permissioned Domains over per-line authorization.

capabilities.name: DisallowIncoming flags
capabilities.summary: A family of account flags that block specific unsolicited inbound objects: asfDisallowIncomingCheck (13), asfDisallowIncomingNFTokenOffer (12), asfDisallowIncomingPayChan (14), asfDisallowIncomingTrustline (15), plus the older asfDisallowXRP (3, advisory) and asfRequireDest (1). They reduce spam/attack surface and let a compliance-managed account refuse object types it does not support, complementing DepositAuth's payment block.
gotchas: asfDisallowXRP (3) is advisory only — it is a hint to wallets/UIs and is NOT enforced by the protocol; do not rely on it to actually block XRP.
The four DisallowIncoming* flags require the DisallowIncoming amendment to be enabled.
asfRequireDest forces a destination tag on incoming payments — useful for shared/custodial accounts but will reject legitimate payments missing a tag.
These block object creation, not identity — they are hygiene/anti-spam controls, not a KYC mechanism.

capabilities.name: Compliance freeze controls (Freeze / Deep Freeze / Clawback)
capabilities.summary: Issuer-side enforcement tools that satisfy AML/sanctions requirements after issuance. Global Freeze (asfGlobalFreeze, 7) freezes all of an issuer's assets; individual freeze locks a single trust line; Deep Freeze additionally blocks the frozen holder from sending or trading on the DEX. Clawback (asfAllowTrustLineClawback, 16) lets the issuer recover issued tokens from a holder. asfNoFreeze (6) permanently relinquishes freeze power for credibly neutral assets.
gotchas: asfNoFreeze is irreversible — once set, the issuer can never freeze again; choosing it forecloses future compliance enforcement.
Clawback (asfAllowTrustLineClawback, 16) must be enabled before issuance and is mutually exclusive with NoFreeze; you cannot have both credibly-neutral and clawback-able.
Deep Freeze (DeepFreeze amendment) goes beyond ordinary freeze by blocking the holder from payments AND DEX activity — verify the amendment is enabled before relying on it.
These are post-hoc enforcement, not access prevention — pair with RequireAuth/Credentials to control entry rather than only reacting after the fact.

best_for.purpose: Sanctions/AML enforcement on a regulated issued asset

research.domain: XRPL node software, API servers, public RPC providers, explorers, wallets, oracles, indexers, client SDKs, and dev networks
research.notes: Mid-2026 synthesis. The XRPL infra stack is now clearly two-tiered: rippled (the consensus/transaction node, currently on the 3.x line after the 3.0.0 release that fixed token/escrow/price handling) and Clio (the read-optimized API server that serves historical data from designated rippled nodes using ~4x less storage). Most app traffic should hit Clio (or a managed provider) for reads and a rippled node for submit/fee. Two milestones reshaped the landscape since the knowledge cutoff: (1) XLS-47 native Price Oracles went LIVE on Mainnet on 2024-11-02 with Band Protocol and DIA as live providers — oracles are no longer a proposal; they back AMM/lending pricing on-chain. (2) The XRPL EVM Sidechain went LIVE on Mainnet on 2025-06-30 (chain ID 1440000, RPC https://rpc.xrplevm.org, XRP as gas, Axelar bridge), giving Solidity/EVM tooling a first-class home connected to XRPL. Wallets consolidated around Xaman (the XUMM rebrand, mobile-first, deepest XRPL feature coverage), GemWallet and Crossmark (browser extensions for dApp signing). Hooks (L1 programmability) remain Xahau-only and NOT on Mainnet; native WASM smart contracts (XLS-100d) and the Lending protocol (XLS-66d) are still on dedicated devnets. Public Ripple servers (s1/s2) are explicitly not for production; serious builders run their own rippled+Clio or use managed providers (QuickNode, GetBlock). WARNING surfaced during research: numerous scam 'airdrop', 'wXRP bridge', and clone-DEX sites impersonate GemWallet/XRPL — always verify against official repos (XRPLF GitHub) and canonical domains (xrpl.org, xaman.app, xrpscan.com, bithomp.com, xrplevm.org).

capabilities.name: rippled (core XRPL server)
capabilities.summary: rippled is the reference C++ server that forms the XRPL peer-to-peer network: it processes transactions, participates in consensus, and can run as a tracking/full node or as a validator. The current line is 3.x (3.0.0 resolved data-processing issues around tokens, escrow, and price). Running your own rippled is the trust-minimized path for transaction submission and fee/server-state queries, and is required if you want to validate. Full-history requires substantial disk; most teams run a tracking node with limited history and pair it with Clio for reads.
key_fields: admin vs public ports (51234 RPC / 6006 WS / 51235 peer)
gotchas: Full-history nodes need terabytes of fast SSD and aggressive online_delete tuning; do not assume a default node keeps history.
Validators must keep keys offline (validator-keys-tool) and use a separate exposed node — never validate directly on a public-facing box.
Operators must upgrade promptly when a new major (e.g. 3.0.0) ships or risk amendment-blocked / desync.
submit and fee require P2P reachability — a read-only Clio cannot replace it.
Public Ripple servers (s1/s2) are rate-limited and not for production.

best_for.purpose: Trust-minimized transaction submission / self-hosted backend
Running a validator to support the network
Authoritative source for amendment/feature availability

capabilities.name: Clio (read-optimized API server)
capabilities.summary: Clio is the XRPLF API server purpose-built for reads: it ingests validated ledger/transaction data from designated rippled nodes and stores it in Cassandra/ScyllaDB using up to 4x less space than rippled, enabling scalable read throughput and HA clusters that share one dataset. It exposes the full rippled API but defaults to validated data; requests needing the P2P network (fee, submit, current ledger) are auto-forwarded to a backing rippled. Pair Clio with rippled for any data-heavy app instead of hammering a rippled node with account_tx/book_offers queries.

gotchas: Clio defaults ledger_index to 'validated' — add ledger_index:'current' to read pending/non-validated state.
Clio cannot submit transactions itself; it forwards to a rippled node which must be reachable.
Backfilling full history into Cassandra/Scylla is operationally heavy; budget storage and ingestion time.
Clio only has data from the point its backing rippled started supplying it — it is not magically full-history unless fed full-history.

best_for.purpose: High-throughput read API (account_tx, NFT, AMM, book_offers)
Backing a wallet/explorer/analytics product

capabilities.name: XLS-47 Native Price Oracles
capabilities.summary: XLS-47 (author Gregory Tsipenyuk) added native price oracles to the XRPL via the PriceOracle amendment, LIVE on Mainnet since 2024-11-02. Off-chain providers publish prices on-chain through OracleSet (create/modify) and OracleDelete transactions, stored in a PriceOracle ledger object (up to 10 base/quote pairs each, scaledPrice = price x 10^scale, scale 0-20). Apps read aggregated values via the get_aggregate_price method (mean/median/trimmed-mean across multiple oracles to reduce single-source risk). Band Protocol and DIA are live integrated providers feeding DeFi (AMM, lending) pricing.
gotchas: Oracles are only as trustworthy as their providers — always query multiple oracles and use get_aggregate_price with trimming, not a single source.
Check LastUpdateTime / freshness before trusting a price; stale feeds are a known DeFi attack surface.
fixPriceOracleOrder (a follow-up bug-fix amendment) was Open for Voting as of mid-2026 — verify its status if asset-pair ordering matters to you.
Scale handling (10^scale) is easy to get wrong; misreading scale produces order-of-magnitude price errors.

best_for.purpose: On-chain price feeds for AMM/lending/DeFi logic

research.domain: Native non-fungible tokens on the XRP Ledger (XLS-20 family)
research.notes: As of mid-2026 the XRPL has a mature native NFT stack, all live on Mainnet. The foundation is XLS-20, enabled by the NonFungibleTokensV1_1 amendment on 2022-10-31 (a roll-up of the original NonFungibleTokensV1 plus the fixNFTokenDirV1 and fixNFTokenNegOffer bug fixes, both now folded in / marked obsolete as standalone amendments). NFTs are first-class ledger objects (NFTokens) stored in NFTokenPage objects (up to 32 per page), not smart-contract tokens, so there is no per-NFT contract risk and minting/trading are protocol-native transactions: NFTokenMint, NFTokenBurn, NFTokenCreateOffer, NFTokenAcceptOffer (direct + brokered), NFTokenCancelOffer. Since 2022 three more NFT amendments have shipped to Mainnet: fixNFTokenRemint (safe sequence numbering via FirstNFTSequence to prevent re-mint collisions), NFTokenMintOffer (mint + place a sell offer in one transaction), and DynamicNFT / XLS-46 (enabled 2025-06-11) which adds the tfMutable flag and the NFTokenModify transaction so an issuer or authorized minter can update an NFT's URI after mint. Royalties are enforced at the protocol level via an immutable TransferFee set at mint (0-50000 = 0.00%-50.00% in 0.001% steps). Collections are convention-based via the 32-bit NFTokenTaxon (no native collection object). For game studios the standout properties are: cheap reserves (one 0.2 XRP NFTokenPage holds up to 32 assets, ~1/12 XRP per NFT amortized), enforced royalties on secondary sales, authorized-minter delegation (mint into a studio issuer account from a separate signing key), batch minting (up to ~200/tx via tickets), and mutable URIs for evolving/upgradeable items. Note: the Batch amendment (multi-tx atomic submission) had a bug and was removed in rippled v3.1.1, so do not rely on it yet.

capabilities.name: XLS-20 Native NFTokens
capabilities.summary: XLS-20 is the protocol-native NFT standard for the XRP Ledger, enabled on Mainnet by the NonFungibleTokensV1_1 amendment on 2022-10-31. NFTokens are first-class ledger objects (not smart-contract tokens), so there is no per-collection contract to deploy or audit and the mint/trade lifecycle is handled by dedicated transaction types. This is the foundation every other NFT capability on XRPL builds on.
capabilities.key_fields: NFToken object holds NFTokenID, URI, and immutable flags. NFTokenID is a 256-bit value encoding: 16-bit Flags + 16-bit TransferFee + 160-bit issuer AccountID + 32-bit NFTokenTaxon + 32-bit Sequence. Requires the NonFungibleTokensV1_1 amendment (rolls in fixNFTokenDirV1 + fixNFTokenNegOffer).
capabilities.gotchas: Flags, TransferFee, issuer, and taxon are baked into the NFTokenID at mint and are immutable forever (only the URI can change, and only if minted mutable). There is no native on-chain collection object. NFTs are not divisible and cannot be used for payments.

best_for.purpose: Issue unique digital collectibles without deploying a contract

capabilities.name: NFTokenMint
capabilities.summary: NFTokenMint creates a new NFToken and assigns it to the minting account (or to the Issuer if minting on behalf via authorized minter). It sets the immutable properties of the NFT: flags, transfer fee, taxon, and URI. This is the single entry point for putting a new NFT on the ledger.
capabilities.key_fields: NFTokenTaxon (required, 0-0xFFFFFFFF collection id), URI (optional, up to 256 bytes hex, not validated), TransferFee (0-50000 = 0%-50% in 0.001% steps), Issuer (optional, for authorized-minter mode), Flags. Flags: tfBurnable 0x1, tfOnlyXRP 0x2, tfTransferable 0x8, tfMutable 0x10. Optional Amount/Destination/Expiration to also create a sell offer (NFTokenMintOffer).
capabilities.gotchas: Flags and TransferFee are permanent once minted. TransferFee only takes effect if tfTransferable is set. URI is stored as hex and never checked for validity, so dead links are possible. Each mint increments the issuer's MintedNFTokens; with fixNFTokenRemint, sequence = FirstNFTSequence + MintedNFTokens. Max NFTs per issuer is 2^32-1.

best_for.purpose: Mint game items, characters, or cosmetics with enforced royalties

capabilities.name: NFTokenBurn
capabilities.summary: NFTokenBurn permanently destroys an NFToken, removing it from the ledger and freeing the owner reserve once the NFTokenPage empties. The current holder can always burn their own NFT; if the token was minted with tfBurnable, the issuer (or authorized minter) can also burn it even when held by another account.
capabilities.key_fields: NFTokenID (required), Owner (only needed when burning a tfBurnable token held by an account other than the signer). Burning also reduces the owner's NFToken count and can shrink/remove NFTokenPage objects.
capabilities.gotchas: Issuer-side burn only works if the NFT carried the tfBurnable flag at mint. Burning is irreversible. For game item sinks (crafting consumption, decay) you must decide burnability at mint time, not later.

best_for.purpose: Item sinks / consumables / crafting in game economies

capabilities.name: NFTokenCreateOffer
capabilities.summary: NFTokenCreateOffer posts either a sell offer (current owner offering to sell) or a buy offer (someone offering to buy) for a specific NFTokenID. Each offer becomes an NFTokenOffer ledger object that costs owner reserve until accepted, cancelled, or expired. The optional Destination field restricts who may accept the offer, which is the mechanism behind targeted and brokered sales.
capabilities.key_fields: NFTokenID (required), Amount (XRP or IOU; can be 0 only for XRP give-away sell offers), Owner (required for buy offers, must differ from Account; omitted for sell offers), Destination (optional, restricts who can accept), Expiration (optional Unix-epoch), Flags: tfSellNFToken 0x1.
capabilities.gotchas: Offers do NOT auto-clean on expiration; an expired offer still occupies a ledger object and reserve until someone runs NFTokenCancelOffer. Sell offers must omit Owner; buy offers must set Owner. Each open offer holds 0.2 XRP of reserve, so high-volume marketplaces accumulate cleanup debt.

best_for.purpose: List items on a marketplace (sell offers)
Targeted player-to-player trades via Destination

capabilities.name: NFTokenAcceptOffer (Direct + Brokered)
capabilities.summary: NFTokenAcceptOffer settles a sale. In direct mode a buyer accepts a sell offer (or a seller accepts a buy offer) by referencing one offer. In brokered mode a third party supplies BOTH a sell offer and a buy offer and matches them, keeping an optional NFTokenBrokerFee; the NFT transfers directly seller-to-buyer and the broker never takes custody. This is the core settlement primitive for any XRPL NFT marketplace.
capabilities.key_fields: NFTokenSellOffer and/or NFTokenBuyOffer (one for direct, both for brokered), NFTokenBrokerFee (brokered only, the cut the broker keeps). Settlement order: buyer debited first, broker credited, then seller. Issuer TransferFee/royalty is applied automatically on top.
capabilities.gotchas: Brokered: both offers must reference the same NFTokenID and the same currency/asset or it fails with tecNFTOKEN_BUY_SELL_MISMATCH. The broker fee must leave the seller at least the amount in their sell offer (before transfer fee). Royalty (issuer TransferFee) is deducted from proceeds automatically and is NOT optional. Broker never owns the NFT.

best_for.purpose: Settle NFT sales on a marketplace
Run a brokered marketplace that takes a fee without custody

capabilities.name: NFTokenCancelOffer
capabilities.summary: NFTokenCancelOffer removes one or more existing NFTokenOffer objects, reclaiming their owner reserve. Because offers (including expired ones) persist as ledger objects, cancellation is the housekeeping primitive that keeps reserve usage and the offer book clean.
capabilities.key_fields: NFTokenOffers (array of offer object IDs to cancel; up to 500). An offer can be cancelled by its creator, by the account named in its Destination, or by anyone if the offer has expired.
capabilities.gotchas: Expired offers are not auto-removed; you must cancel them to free the 0.2 XRP reserve each holds. Cancelling many at once (up to 500) is the standard cleanup pattern. Anyone may cancel an already-expired offer, which marketplaces use to garbage-collect.

capabilities.name: Transfer Fees / Royalties
capabilities.summary: XRPL enforces creator royalties at the protocol level via the TransferFee field set at mint. The value ranges 0-50000, representing 0.00%-50.00% in 0.001% increments, and the fee is automatically deducted from secondary-sale proceeds and paid to the issuer. Unlike contract-based royalties on other chains, this cannot be bypassed by marketplaces because settlement happens in the protocol.
capabilities.key_fields: TransferFee (UInt16, 0-50000). Only effective when tfTransferable is set. Encoded into the NFTokenID (the 16 bits after Flags). Royalty is taken from the sale amount before the seller is credited, in both direct and brokered NFTokenAcceptOffer.
capabilities.gotchas: TransferFee is immutable after mint and only applies to transferable NFTs. Royalties are paid to the ISSUER address, so for authorized-minter setups confirm the issuer is the account that should receive royalties (a minter can hold the NFT while royalties still flow to the issuer). First-sale/direct issuer transactions are not subject to the transfer fee.

best_for.purpose: Guarantee creator royalties that marketplaces cannot strip

capabilities.name: NFTokenTaxon & Collections
capabilities.summary: Collections on XRPL are convention-based, not a native ledger object. Each NFT carries a 32-bit NFTokenTaxon (0x0-0xFFFFFFFF) chosen by the minter to group related NFTs; marketplaces and indexers filter by issuer + taxon to render a collection. There is no enforced collection metadata, supply cap, or uniqueness on taxon at the protocol level.
capabilities.key_fields: NFTokenTaxon (UInt32, required on every mint; set 0 if unused). Encoded into the NFTokenID. Internally the ledger scrambles the taxon using the sequence as a PRNG seed so NFTs spread across NFTokenPage objects (you still read back the original taxon via parseNFTokenID).
capabilities.gotchas: No on-chain collection object means no native floor price, supply cap, or collection-level metadata; anyone can mint with any taxon, so 'collection authenticity' is established by the issuer address, not the taxon alone. Always verify issuer + taxon together. The stored taxon value is scrambled on-ledger but decoded transparently by libraries (parseNFTokenID).

best_for.purpose: Group items into sets/series for marketplace display
Organize game asset families (weapons, skins, characters)

capabilities.name: NFTokenPage & Owner Reserve
capabilities.summary: NFTs are stored in NFTokenPage objects, each holding up to 32 NFTs owned by the same account. Owner reserve is charged per page (currently 0.2 XRP), not per NFT, which makes XRPL NFTs extremely cheap to hold at scale: assuming ~24 NFTs per page on average, the cost amortizes to roughly 1/12 XRP (~0.0167 XRP) per NFT. The base account reserve is 1 XRP since the December 2024 reduction.
capabilities.key_fields: NFTokenPage holds up to 32 NFTs; owner reserve 0.2 XRP per page; base reserve 1 XRP per account. Rule of thumb: reserve for N NFTs is approximately (0.2 * N) / 24 XRP. Pages are keyed and split automatically as an account accumulates NFTs.
capabilities.gotchas: Reserve is per page, so the marginal cost of an NFT is zero until a page fills and a new one is created, then it jumps 0.2 XRP. Selling/burning NFTs can free a page and return reserve. Reserve values are network parameters and can change by fee vote (they dropped sharply in Dec 2024). Plan reserve budgeting around pages, not NFT counts.

capabilities.name: Dynamic / Mutable NFTs (dNFTs)
capabilities.summary: The DynamicNFT amendment (XLS-46d), enabled on Mainnet 2025-06-11, lets an issuer mint mutable NFTs whose URI can be changed after issuance. Mint with the tfMutable flag (0x10), then use the new NFTokenModify transaction to update the URI. This unlocks evolving metadata such as upgradeable game items, athlete cards with live stats, or tickets whose details change, without re-minting.
capabilities.key_fields: tfMutable flag (0x10) on NFTokenMint marks an NFT as mutable. NFTokenModify transaction (fields: NFTokenID, Owner if not the signer, new URI) updates the URI. Only the issuer or their authorized minter may modify. Requires the DynamicNFT amendment and rippled v2.4.0+.
capabilities.gotchas: Only the URI is mutable; flags, taxon, and transfer fee remain permanently fixed. Mutability must be chosen at mint (tfMutable) and cannot be added later; non-mutable NFTs can never be modified. Only the issuer/authorized minter can call NFTokenModify, not the current holder. Servers below v2.4.0 are amendment-blocked.

best_for.purpose: Upgradeable / leveling game items with evolving metadata
NFTs whose off-chain data changes over time (tickets, cards, status)

capabilities.name: Authorized Minter Delegation
capabilities.summary: An issuer can authorize a separate account to mint NFTs on its behalf by setting the NFTokenMinter field with the asfAuthorizedNFTokenMinter flag via AccountSet. The minter signs NFTokenMint with the Issuer field set to the authorizing account; royalties (TransferFee) still flow to the issuer. This separates a cold issuer identity from a hot signing key and lets a studio or platform mint for a brand.
capabilities.key_fields: AccountSet with NFTokenMinter = <minter address> and asfAuthorizedNFTokenMinter flag set (clear the flag to revoke). The minter then submits NFTokenMint with Issuer = <issuer address>. Only one authorized minter per issuer at a time. Authorized minter can also burn/modify tfBurnable/tfMutable NFTs of that issuer.
capabilities.gotchas: Only ONE authorized minter per issuer at a time; setting a new one replaces the old. Royalties always go to the Issuer, not the minter, so a platform can mint and even hold the NFT while the brand collects royalties. Revoking the minter does not affect already-minted NFTs. Keep the issuer key cold; treat the minter key as operational/hot.

capabilities.name: Batch Minting & NFTokenMintOffer
capabilities.summary: Two patterns for scaling supply. Batch minting submits many NFTokenMint transactions efficiently using pre-created Tickets (XRPL tutorials cap UI batches around 200 per run) so a studio can drop a whole collection. The NFTokenMintOffer amendment (enabled on Mainnet) goes further by letting a single NFTokenMint transaction also place a sell offer (via Amount/Destination/Expiration), halving the transaction count for list-on-mint drops.
capabilities.key_fields: Batch mint: pre-create Tickets, then fire N NFTokenMint transactions (each consuming a ticket) in parallel without sequence contention; tutorials demonstrate up to ~200/run. NFTokenMintOffer: NFTokenMint with Amount (+ optional Destination, Expiration) creates the NFT and its sell offer atomically. Note: this is distinct from the unrelated Batch amendment, which was removed in rippled v3.1.1.
capabilities.gotchas: Do NOT confuse NFTokenMintOffer (mint+offer in one tx, live) with the general Batch amendment (multi-tx atomic bundles) which had a bug and was removed in v3.1.1 - do not rely on Batch yet. Ticket-based batch minting needs enough tickets pre-created and enough reserve. fixNFTokenRemint changed sequence derivation (FirstNFTSequence + MintedNFTokens), so plan IDs accordingly.

research.domain: XRPL native payment primitives — direct, conditional, deferred, channelized, and cross-currency value movement
research.notes: As of mid-2026 the XRPL advanced-payments surface is broad and production-mature. The base Payment transaction handles direct XRP, token, and cross-currency (auto-bridged via DEX/AMM) transfers. The headline 2026 change: the TokenEscrow amendment (XLS-85) went LIVE on mainnet 2026-02-12 (shipped in rippled v3.0.0, with the fixTokenEscrowV1 companion amendment correcting an MPT transfer-fee accounting bug), so Escrow now supports issued tokens (IOUs) and Multi-Purpose Tokens (MPTs) — not just XRP — provided issuers opt in via flags (lsfAllowTrustLineLocking for IOUs; tfMPTCanEscrow + tfMPTCanTransfer for MPTs). Payment Channels remain XRP-ONLY (no token support) and are the canonical off-ledger micropayment/streaming primitive. Checks (deferred pull-style payments) support both XRP and tokens. The single most important developer caveat across the whole lane is the partial-payment exploit: never trust the Amount/DeliverMax field of a delivered Payment — always read the delivered_amount metadata field. The Amount field was renamed DeliverMax in rippled API v2 specifically to blunt this footgun. Cross-currency payments depend on pathfinding over the DEX order books + AMMs; always pathfind and confirm before signing.

capabilities.name: Payment transaction (direct & cross-currency)
capabilities.summary: The core value-transfer transaction on the XRPL. Sends XRP, issued tokens (IOUs), or MPTs from one account to another, and can perform cross-currency conversions automatically by routing through the decentralized exchange (order books + AMMs) when SendMax and Amount specify different currencies. It is the foundation every other payment pattern builds on or settles into.
key_fields: Amount / DeliverMax (in API v2 the field was renamed from Amount to DeliverMax)
SendMax (max source-currency to spend; required for cross-currency)
DeliverMin (minimum to deliver, used with partial payments)
gotchas: NEVER read the Amount/DeliverMax field to determine what was actually received — read the delivered_amount metadata field (see partial-payment caveat).
Cross-currency sends require SendMax and benefit from a separate pathfinding step before signing; rippled may not always find the cheapest path.
Sending tokens to a Destination with no trust line for that currency fails unless it is a return to the issuer.
If the destination has RequireDest enabled, omitting DestinationTag fails the transaction.

best_for.purpose: Direct XRP transfer
Issuing / sending stablecoins and IOUs
Cross-currency settlement via DEX/AMM
In-game soft/hard currency transfers

sources.claim: Cross-currency payments default to using the order book or AMM between the SendMax source currency and the Amount destination currency.

capabilities.name: Partial payments (tfPartialPayment) & delivered_amount
capabilities.summary: The tfPartialPayment flag lets a Payment succeed by reducing the amount the recipient receives rather than increasing the amount the sender pays — useful for returning funds, paying through illiquid paths, or sweeping dust. It is the source of the most notorious XRPL integration exploit: a malicious sender sets a large Amount with the partial-payment flag, the payment delivers a tiny fraction, and a naive integrator that reads Amount credits the full advertised value. The defense is mandatory: always use the delivered_amount metadata field.
key_fields: DeliverMin (floor on delivery when using partial payments)
delivered_amount (metadata field — the authoritative actual amount delivered)
Amount / DeliverMax (the CAP, not the delivered amount)
gotchas: THE EXPLOIT: never assume the Amount/DeliverMax field equals what was delivered on a successful (tesSUCCESS) partial payment — read delivered_amount in the transaction metadata.
delivered_amount returns the string 'unavailable' for some very old (pre-2014) transactions; handle that case.
The field rename to DeliverMax (rippled API v2) exists specifically to reduce this misreading — but old integrations and old API versions still surface Amount.
tfPartialPayment cannot be used to deliver MORE than Amount; it only ever reduces delivery.

best_for.purpose: Exchange/custody deposit crediting (defensively)
Returning funds through thin liquidity
Dust sweeping / fee-absorbed payouts

capabilities.name: Cross-currency payments & pathfinding
capabilities.summary: Pathfinding finds the most cost-effective route for a payment that converts between currencies, using the XRPL's native decentralized exchange (order books) and Automated Market Makers. A Payment carries a path set (a collection of candidate paths sharing the same start and end currency); a single transaction can combine liquidity across multiple paths and intermediaries. Builders use the ripple_path_find / path_find RPC methods to compute paths off-transaction, then submit with SendMax and the resulting Paths.
gotchas: Liquidity shifts every few ledgers (~3–5s); a path found now may be stale at submission — pathfind close to signing and set SendMax to bound cost.
rippled is NOT guaranteed to find the cheapest path; confirm results before signing.
Without trust-line rippling configured correctly, intermediary IOU steps may not flow (No Ripple flag interactions).
Auto-bridging through XRP can route token-to-token trades; XLS-60d DefaultAutoBridge work affects default bridging behavior.

best_for.purpose: Pay in one currency, deliver another
FX / remittance corridors
Accept many tokens, settle to one treasury currency

capabilities.name: Destination tags & source tags
capabilities.summary: Source and destination tags are 32-bit unsigned integers attached to payments (and other transactions like escrows and checks) that let a single receiving address disambiguate among many logical beneficiaries. Exchanges, custodians, and payment processors rely on destination tags to credit the correct customer when many users share one hosted wallet. Accounts can require destination tags via the RequireDest account flag to prevent misrouted deposits.
key_fields: Account flag: asfRequireDest / RequireDestTag (tfRequireDestTag in AccountSet)
X-addresses (encode address + tag together to reduce user error)
gotchas: Omitting a required DestinationTag on an account with RequireDest enabled fails the transaction (tecDST_TAG_NEEDED).
Tags are NOT encrypted or validated by the ledger — they are application-level routing hints; the receiving business must map them.
A wrong or missing tag to an exchange is the #1 cause of 'lost' deposits; prefer X-addresses to bundle address+tag and avoid copy errors.
Tags are distinct from InvoiceID — tags route to a beneficiary, InvoiceID references an external order/invoice.

best_for.purpose: Shared/hosted-wallet deposit routing
Per-customer crediting at an exchange/PSP
Player account attribution to a single game treasury

capabilities.name: Invoice ID (InvoiceID field)
capabilities.summary: InvoiceID is an optional 256-bit (64 hex char) field on Payment and Check transactions used to reference an external invoice, order, or off-ledger document. It is arbitrary application-defined data — typically a hash of an invoice — that lets merchants and payment systems reconcile an on-ledger payment against a specific order. Unlike a destination tag, it carries no routing semantics.
key_fields: appears on Payment and CheckCreate transactions
commonly set to a SHA-256 hash of an external invoice
gotchas: The ledger does not interpret or enforce InvoiceID — it is opaque payload for the application layer.
It is fixed-width 256-bit hex; pad/hash arbitrary order IDs to fit.
Do not use it as a routing mechanism — that is the destination tag's job.
Putting sensitive plaintext in InvoiceID leaks it permanently to the public ledger; store a hash instead.

best_for.purpose: Reconcile on-ledger payment to off-ledger invoice
Order/receipt attestation for compliance

capabilities.name: Escrow (XRP) — time-based & conditional
capabilities.summary: Escrow locks XRP on-ledger to be released only when conditions are met. Three release models exist: time-based (FinishAfter), conditional (a PREIMAGE-SHA-256 crypto-condition whose fulfillment must be supplied), and combination (both). EscrowCreate locks the funds, EscrowFinish releases them to the destination once conditions hold, and EscrowCancel returns them to the sender after CancelAfter expiry. It is trustless, smart-contract-free conditional payment built into the protocol.
key_fields: EscrowCreate: Amount, Destination, FinishAfter, CancelAfter, Condition (PREIMAGE-SHA-256), DestinationTag
gotchas: PREIMAGE-SHA-256 is the ONLY supported crypto-condition type.
EscrowFinish with a Fulfillment costs an elevated fee proportional to the fulfillment size (anti-spam).
Release times are granular to ledger close (~3–5s); FinishAfter is 'earliest', not exact.
An escrow without FinishAfter or Condition is pointless (would be immediately finishable); the ledger requires at least one release mechanism.
Locked XRP still counts toward the owner's reserve obligations.

best_for.purpose: Conditional / milestone payments
Time-locked vesting or holdbacks
Hash-locked cross-chain / HTLC-style swaps
In-game reward escrow / tournament prize locks

capabilities.name: Token Escrow (XLS-85) — IOU & MPT escrow
capabilities.summary: The 2026 flagship payments upgrade: the TokenEscrow amendment (XLS-85) extends Escrow beyond XRP to issued tokens (IOUs / Trust Line tokens such as RLUSD) and Multi-Purpose Tokens (MPTs). It went live on XRPL mainnet on 2026-02-12 (shipped in rippled v3.0.0, paired with fixTokenEscrowV1 which corrected an MPT transfer-fee accounting bug). This lets stablecoins and tokenized assets be locked under protocol-level conditions without smart contracts — a key enabler for TradFi custody and tokenized-treasury workflows.
key_fields: Same EscrowCreate/Finish/Cancel transactions, with Amount now accepting an issued-token or MPT object
CancelAfter is REQUIRED for token escrows
Issuer opt-in flags: lsfAllowTrustLineLocking (IOU issuer) ; tfMPTCanEscrow + tfMPTCanTransfer (MPT issuer)
fixTokenEscrowV1 companion amendment (MPT transfer-fee accounting fix)
gotchas: Issuers MUST opt in: IOU issuers set Allow Trust Line Locking; MPT issuers set Can Escrow + Can Transfer — without these, token escrows are rejected.
CancelAfter is mandatory for token escrows (unlike XRP escrows where it is optional).
Sender and recipient may need to be pre-authorized by the token issuer (authorized trust lines / MPT authorization).
Deep-frozen or locked token holders cannot finish escrows.
fixTokenEscrowV1 is required to avoid an MPT issuer locked-balance miscalculation when transfer fees apply — ensure the network has it (it ships with v3.0.0).

best_for.purpose: Stablecoin (RLUSD) conditional/escrowed settlement
Tokenized-treasury / RWA custody locks
Token vesting and milestone releases
In-game token holdbacks / marketplace escrow

capabilities.name: Crypto-conditions (PREIMAGE-SHA-256)
capabilities.summary: Crypto-conditions are the cryptographic locking mechanism used by conditional Escrow. The XRPL implements the IETF crypto-conditions draft but supports exactly one type: PREIMAGE-SHA-256, a hash-lock. The escrow creator publishes a Condition (the SHA-256 hash); the party that knows the preimage supplies it as the Fulfillment in EscrowFinish to release funds. This is the building block for Hash Time-Locked Contracts (HTLCs) and atomic cross-chain swaps on XRPL.
key_fields: generated with the five-bells-condition library or equivalent
fee on EscrowFinish scales with Fulfillment size
gotchas: Only PREIMAGE-SHA-256 is supported — RSA/ED25519/THRESHOLD condition types from the IETF draft are NOT implemented.
Lose the preimage and the funds are unrecoverable until CancelAfter lets the sender reclaim them.
The Condition/Fulfillment must be correctly DER/hex-encoded; malformed values fail with temMALFORMED.
EscrowFinish with a fulfillment carries a higher fee proportional to fulfillment length.

best_for.purpose: Hash-locked escrow (HTLC)
Atomic cross-chain swaps
Reveal-secret-to-release flows

capabilities.name: Payment Channels (PaymentChannelCreate / Fund / Claim)
capabilities.summary: Payment Channels enable asynchronous, off-ledger XRP micropayments that settle on-ledger with a single transaction. The payer creates a channel (PaymentChannelCreate) escrowing XRP, then issues digitally signed claims off-ledger without touching consensus; the payee verifies each claim with the channel_verify method and later redeems the cumulative balance with PaymentChannelClaim. This is the canonical primitive for streaming payments, pay-per-use APIs, and high-frequency micropayments (Ed25519 keys allow >100k signature verifications/sec).
key_fields: PaymentChannelCreate: Amount, Destination, SettleDelay, PublicKey, CancelAfter, DestinationTag
PaymentChannelClaim: Channel, Balance, Amount, Signature, PublicKey, Flags (tfClose, tfRenew)
off-ledger signed claim (channel id + cumulative amount)
gotchas: XRP ONLY — payment channels do NOT support issued tokens or MPTs (unlike Escrow after XLS-85).
The payee must redeem claims before the channel expires or those funds return to the payer.
Two expirations: mutable Expiration (set/extended via Fund) and immutable CancelAfter (fixed at creation).
Claims are cumulative (monotonic), not incremental — each signed claim states the total authorized balance, so only the highest claim matters.
Use Ed25519 keys for the channel to maximize verification throughput for streaming use cases.

best_for.purpose: Streaming / pay-per-second micropayments
Pay-per-use API metering
High-frequency low-value game transactions
Creator-tipping by listening/viewing time

capabilities.name: Checks (CheckCreate / CheckCash / CheckCancel)
capabilities.summary: Checks are deferred, pull-style payments: the sender writes a Check authorizing a maximum amount, and the recipient later pulls funds by cashing it. CheckCreate defines the destination, an optional expiration, and a SendMax cap; CheckCash lets the destination redeem an exact amount or a flexible (up-to-max) amount; CheckCancel voids an unredeemed check. Unlike Escrow, funds are NOT locked at creation — the check only succeeds at cash time if the sender still holds sufficient balance. Checks support both XRP and issued tokens.
key_fields: CheckCreate: Destination, SendMax (max debitable), Expiration, DestinationTag, InvoiceID
CheckCash: CheckID, Amount (exact) OR DeliverMin (flexible up-to-max)
gotchas: Funds are NOT escrowed — a check can fail at cash time if the sender's balance dropped below SendMax.
Only the Destination can cash a check; either party can cancel.
Cashing for a token requires the destination to have a trust line for that currency.
An expired check can only be canceled, not cashed.
Lower adoption than Escrow/Payment Channels — verify your target wallets/tooling support Checks before relying on them.

best_for.purpose: Deferred / pull-based payments (recipient-initiated)
Authorize-now, collect-later invoicing
B2B payment authorization with later settlement

sources.title: CheckCash — Transaction Types (xrpl.org)
sources.claim: CheckCash redeems a Check for up to the authorized maximum; only the Destination address can cash it, choosing an exact Amount or a flexible DeliverMin.

research.domain: EVM smart contracts on an XRP-gas Cosmos L1 sidechain, bridged to XRPL mainnet via Axelar
research.notes: As of mid-2026 the XRPL EVM sidechain is a LIVE, distinct Layer 1 — its mainnet launched 2025-06-30 (announced at EthCC) and is the home for Solidity/EVM smart contracts in the XRP ecosystem, which the native XRP Ledger deliberately does NOT support. It is a standalone Cosmos-SDK chain (CometBFT / Proof-of-Authority consensus, migrated from the Evmos stack to Cosmos EVM v0.4.1) built by Ripple + Peersyst + Axelar, with XRP itself as the native gas token. EVM mainnet chain ID is 1440000 (RPC https://rpc.xrplevm.org, explorer https://explorer.xrplevm.org); testnet is 1449000. It exposes the standard Ethereum JSON-RPC, so MetaMask, Hardhat, Foundry, Remix, ethers.js and web3.js work unchanged. Cross-chain value moves over Axelar (exclusive launch bridge — Squid Router UI, Interchain Token Service, General Message Passing) plus native Cosmos IBC, with Wormhole integration incoming. Performance: >1,000 TPS, 3-5s blocks, sub-cent fees. The build-decision rule: use the EVM sidechain when you need Turing-complete Solidity/DeFi composability; use native XRPL for cheap built-in payments/DEX/NFTs (XLS-20) and Xahau for Hooks-style lightweight on-ledger logic. Capabilities below carry chain=xrpl-evm-sidechain throughout. Verified against xrplevm.org, docs.xrplevm.org, Ripple insights, Axelar blog, ChainList and QuickNode docs.

capabilities.summary: The XRPL EVM sidechain is a standalone Layer-1 blockchain that runs Ethereum-compatible smart contracts with XRP as the native gas token. Mainnet went live 2025-06-30; it saw ~1,400 contracts deployed in week one.

capabilities.summary: Axelar is the exclusive launch bridge connecting XRPL mainnet to the EVM sidechain and to 80+ other chains. capabilities.name: When to use EVM sidechain vs native XRPL vs Xahau
capabilities.summary: A build-decision rule for placing a feature on the right chain. Use the EVM sidechain when you need Turing-complete Solidity, composable DeFi, or to port Ethereum dApps — XRP-denominated but fully programmable. Use native XRPL mainnet for cheap, battle-tested built-in primitives (payments, the native DEX/AMM, XLS-20 NFTs, escrow, multi-sign) without writing a VM contract. Use Xahau when you want lightweight on-ledger automation (Hooks) closer to XRPL's model without a full EVM.

Native XRPL (xrpl-mainnet): built-in payments, DEX/AMM, XLS-20 NFTs, escrow, low fees, no smart contracts. Xahau: Hooks (lightweight WASM-ish on-ledger logic). Bridge assets between chains via Axelar.
capabilities.gotchas: Don't reimplement on the EVM what XRPL already does natively and cheaply (basic payments, DEX, NFTs) just to stay in Solidity — you lose XRPL's free-tier robustness. Conversely, don't expect XRPL mainnet to run arbitrary contracts — it can't, by design. Cross-chain composition means bridge latency/fees and bridge trust. Xahau Hooks are not EVM — different programming model entirely.

research.domain: On-ledger smart-contract layer (WASM Hooks) on the Xahau network, a Layer-1 fork of XRPL Core
research.notes: As of mid-2026, Hooks are a production feature of the Xahau network (mainnet live since 2023-10-31, network ID 21337) — NOT of XRPL mainnet. XRPL mainnet has no native smart contracts; its programmability roadmap centers on the EVM sidechain (separate lane). Xahau is a distinct Layer-1 chain that forked xrpld/XRPL Core and added the Hooks Amendment, native XAH gas token, a Hook-implemented Governance Game on the genesis account, Balance Rewards (compounding-interest via ClaimReward), URIToken NFTs, the Remit multi-op transaction, and Import-based one-way value transfer from XRPL. Hooks are intentionally NOT Turing-complete: they are small WebAssembly modules attached to accounts that run BEFORE and/or AFTER transactions touch the account, with bounded execution enforced by mandatory loop guards (_g). The canonical authoring language has been C compiled to WASM; Rust (hooks-rs) is experimental; and JavaScript Hooks (JSHooks, via a forked QuickJS-on-WASI runtime, HookApiVersion 1) are the headline 2025–2026 development — running on a dedicated JSHooks testnet (network 31338) and pending audit before a mainnet amendment, so treat JS as testnet-only for production planning. Newer building blocks shipped/voted in this window include CronSet (on-chain scheduled Hook callbacks) and ZeroB2M (which retired Burn-2-Mint asset creation). Docs moved to xahau.network/docs (docs.xahau.network 301-redirects there). When a builder needs custom on-ledger logic in the XRPL family TODAY, Xahau Hooks is the mature path; for EVM/Solidity, use the XRPL EVM sidechain instead.

capabilities.name: Hooks (WASM smart-contract layer)
capabilities.summary: Hooks are small, efficient WebAssembly modules attached to a Xahau account that execute BEFORE and/or AFTER transactions affect that account, letting the account accept, reject, or augment activity with custom logic. They are intentionally NOT Turing-complete — arbitrary unbounded loops are forbidden — which keeps worst-case execution predictable and priceable. Hooks are the native smart-contract primitive of Xahau and have been live on Xahau mainnet since the 2023-10-31 launch. They do NOT exist on XRPL mainnet; that chain has no native programmability layer.
key_fields: hook chain (up to 4 strong hooks per account, sender + receiver)
gotchas: Hooks live ONLY on Xahau, never on XRPL mainnet — a common misconception is that XRPL gained smart contracts; it did not.
A hook is account-scoped, not a global contract — there is no shared global address space like EVM; logic is bound to the account it is installed on.
Execution is bounded and metered; you cannot run open-ended computation.

capabilities.name: SetHook transaction
capabilities.summary: SetHook is the transaction that installs, updates, or removes Hooks on an account. Each entry of its Hooks array is a HookSet object operating on one position of the account's hook chain; CreateCode carries WASM bytecode for a new hook, or HookHash references an existing reference-counted HookDefinition. The same transaction selects operation by field presence and flags: create, install (reuse a HookDefinition), update (change params/namespace/grants only), delete (hsfOVERRIDE + empty CreateCode), and namespace-reset (hsfNSDELETE).
key_fields: HookOn (bitmask of which transaction types fire the hook)
gotchas: Array position MUST match the intended hook-chain position; a no-op (empty object) preserves that slot.
Delete requires hsfOVERRIDE AND an empty CreateCode; getting this wrong silently no-ops instead of deleting.
A parameter is deleted by supplying its name with no value field — not by setting an empty value.
Reference counting prevents deletion of a HookDefinition still referenced by other accounts.
Namespace cleanup (hsfNSDELETE) is capped at 512 HookState entries per transaction.

capabilities.name: Hook API (C primitives / function categories)
capabilities.summary: The Hook API is the set of host functions a hook calls to read the originating transaction, manage state, do math, and emit transactions. It is a low-level C ABI; higher-level SDKs (C macros, Rust, JS) wrap it.

capabilities.name: Guard / weak-guard (_g) and bounded execution
capabilities.summary: Because Hooks are deliberately not Turing-complete, every loop must be guarded: a _g(guard_id, maxiter) call placed as the first branch after the loop instruction declares the maximum iterations the developer promises. If exceeded at runtime the hook auto-rolls back with GUARD_VIOLATION. The ledger uses these guards to compute the worst-case instruction count BEFORE execution, which is the basis for the deterministic execution fee. This is the mechanism that makes hook execution time and cost predictable and DoS-resistant.
key_fields: static analysis at SetHook time rejects unguarded loops
gotchas: A SetHook with an unguarded loop is rejected outright — you cannot deploy it.
maxiter is a hard promise; underestimating it causes runtime GUARD_VIOLATION and a fully rolled-back hook (the transaction the hook guarded can be blocked).
Heavy looping inflates worst-case instruction count and therefore the fee, even if the average run is cheap — fees are charged on the worst case, not the actual path.
