capabilities.name: Hook State (namespaced key-value storage)
capabilities.summary: Hook State is a per-account key-value store that persists data between hook executions. Keys are always 32 bytes (256-bit) and values are variable length up to a validator-voted maximum (256 bytes at time of writing). A 32-byte namespace scopes state so multiple hooks on one account don't clobber each other, and the same key under different namespaces refers to different objects. State consumes owner reserve on a scale (scale 1 = 1 reserve per up-to-256-byte entry; scale 4 = 4 reserve per up-to-1024 bytes).
gotchas: You pay the chosen reserve scale even if an entry holds a single byte — pick the scale up front based on real size needs.
Value max is governance-tuned (256 bytes currently); large blobs must be chunked across keys.
Foreign-state reads require an explicit grant from the owning account; cross-account state is not open by default.
Deleting all state in a namespace at SetHook time is capped at 512 entries per transaction (hsfNSDELETE).

capabilities.name: Emitted transactions (autonomous on-ledger actions)
capabilities.summary: Emitted transactions are brand-new transactions a hook creates and emits() into the next ledger, letting hooks make ledger changes (e.g. send a payment, mint a URIToken) beyond merely accepting/rejecting the originating transaction. The hook must present a fully serialized, canonically-formed transaction (no rewriting by xahaud), with signature replaced by an EmitDetails block (nonce, parent txn id, generation, burden). A cbak() callback fires when the emitted transaction is accepted (or on failure). This is what enables autonomous, reactive on-ledger logic.
gotchas: No rewriting: xahaud will not fill in fields — an incompletely or non-canonically serialized emitted txn fails to emit.
Generation is capped at 10 and burden grows exponentially with depth, so recursive emission chains are hard-bounded.
Emitted transactions must land within ~5 ledgers or they expire and trigger a failure callback.
Nonces are deterministic and network-agreed; do not roll your own randomness for hashes.

capabilities.name: Hook fees & execution metering
capabilities.summary: Hook execution is metered at roughly 1 drop of XAH per WebAssembly instruction in the WORST-CASE execution path (including any cbak callback), so a small but loop-heavy hook can attract high runtime fees. Strong hooks must be paid for by the originator of the transaction; an account can carry up to 4 strong hooks on the sending side and 4 on the receiving side. Combined with guard-derived worst-case counts, this makes fees deterministic and computable before submission — but it means cost is driven by the ceiling, not the average path.

up to 4 strong hooks sender + 4 receiver
owner reserve for installed hooks + state
gotchas: Fee is charged on the guard-declared worst case, NOT the actual executed path — over-broad maxiter inflates cost.
Strong hooks make the SENDER pay for the receiver-side logic in some flows; model who bears the fee.
Loop-heavy hooks can become surprisingly expensive; profile worst-case instruction counts before deploy.

capabilities.name: CronSet (scheduled hook callbacks)
capabilities.summary: CronSet brings on-chain scheduled execution to Xahau — a blockchain alarm clock that wakes a hook and fires its callback at a set time and interval without any external trigger or off-chain service. research.domain: XRPL core protocol: consensus, validators/UNL, ledger structure & objects, fees & reserves, the amendment process, and the XRP native asset
research.notes: As of mid-2026 the XRP Ledger is in an unusually active protocol-evolution phase. The decisive axis is the amendment process: nothing ships to mainnet without >80% validator support sustained for two weeks, and the 2025-2026 window proved the system both fast (PermissionedDomains Feb 2026, MPTokensV1 Oct 2025, DynamicNFT Jun 2025) and self-protecting (the original Batch amendment was killed in validator voting in Feb 2026 after Cantina AI's tooling found a signature-bypass flaw; rippled 3.1.1 marked it unsupported and a corrected BatchV1_1 was proposed). The biggest structural change is operational, not consensus: the core server software is being renamed rippled -> xrpld in v3.2.0 (target June 15 2026) with a 30-40% memory reduction, while Clio (read-optimized API server backed by Cassandra/ScyllaDB) has become the standard way to serve historical/account data so xrpld nodes stay lean. For builders the load-bearing facts are: reserves are currently 1 XRP base + 0.2 XRP/object (set by fee voting, can change), the base tx cost is 10 drops with exponential open-ledger fee escalation under load, and the DeFi primitives (Lending Protocol / Single Asset Vaults via XLS-66/65) entered voting in late Jan 2026 with fixCleanup3_1_3 hardening them on mainnet by late May 2026. Build against validated ledgers, budget for reserves per owned object, and never assume an amendment is live without checking its on-chain status.

capabilities.name: XRP Ledger Consensus Protocol (XRP LCP)
capabilities.summary: XRP LCP is the federated Byzantine agreement protocol that the XRP Ledger uses instead of proof-of-work or proof-of-stake. Its only job is to make trusted validators agree on which set of candidate transactions and their order go into the next ledger; it does not vote on transaction outcomes (those are deterministic given the set). Consensus rounds close a new ledger roughly every 3-5 seconds, and a ledger becomes validated and immutable once a supermajority of a server's trusted validators agree on its hash. Energy-efficient and final-on-validation (no probabilistic confirmations like Bitcoin).
capabilities.key_fields: Validated ledgers (build against ledger_index validated, never current/closed for finality); ledger close ~3-5s; consensus rounds operate in deliberation/establish/accept phases; finality = validated (no reorgs of validated ledgers). API: server_info (validated_ledger, complete_ledgers), ledger with ledger_index: validated.
capabilities.gotchas: current and closed ledgers are NOT final and can change; only validated ledgers are immutable. Consensus agrees on the SET and ORDER of transactions, not their success - a transaction can be validated-and-included yet have a tec result code (failed but fee charged). A small set of trusted validators reaching agreement is what gives finality, so trust assumptions live in the UNL, not in raw hashpower/stake.

best_for.purpose: Fast-finality settlement without mining/staking
Deterministic, low-latency game economy state

capabilities.name: Validators & Unique Node List (UNL)
capabilities.summary: Each XRPL server is configured with a Unique Node List (UNL): the set of validators it trusts not to collude. Only validation votes from UNL members count during consensus; votes from non-UNL validators are ignored. Most operators do not hand-curate a UNL - they subscribe to a published, signed validator list (vl.ripple.com historically, with the network migrating toward an XRPLF-published default UNL in 2025). The UNL is where the network's trust assumptions live: safety depends on UNLs overlapping by a sufficient margin across the network.
capabilities.key_fields: validators.txt config (validator_list_sites, validator_list_keys); signed validator list (vl) with manifests; server_info -> validation_quorum; quorum is ~80% of trusted+available validators. API to inspect: validators, validator_list_sites, manifest.
capabilities.gotchas: Running your own validator does NOT mean others trust you - you must be added to their UNLs / a published vl to influence consensus. UNLs across the network must overlap (>~90% recommended) or the network can fork. The default-UNL publisher key matters: a 2025 migration changed the canonical publisher; ensure servers trust the current XRPLF list. Validators earn no direct protocol reward (no staking yield); they run for ecosystem reasons.

best_for.purpose: Understanding XRPL trust/decentralization model for compliance review

capabilities.name: Negative UNL
capabilities.summary: The Negative UNL is a liveness feature that lets the network keep validating ledgers during a partial outage. When trusted validators go offline, consensus temporarily reduces the effective quorum by disregarding the unreliable validators, so forward progress continues even with several validators down. Validators are added/removed via UNLModify pseudo-transactions at flag ledgers based on a measured reliability threshold (added below ~50% reliability over the last 256 ledgers, removed above ~80%).
capabilities.key_fields: UNLModify pseudo-transaction; flag ledgers (ledger_index % 256 == 0, ~every 15 min); reliability = % of last 256 ledgers where the validator's vote matched consensus; at most one add and one remove per flag ledger; safeguard: quorum can never drop below 60% of total UNL entries; Negative UNL considered 'full' at 25% of configured validators.
capabilities.gotchas: Improves liveness, NOT safety - it does not let a smaller group rewrite history. If MORE than ~20% of validators drop simultaneously, the network may stall on validated ledgers until the Negative UNL adjusts over successive rounds (degrades gracefully for slow 1-2-at-a-time outages, not sudden mass outages). Builders should treat brief validated-ledger gaps during incidents as expected and wait for validated, not panic on current-ledger latency.

best_for.purpose: Reasoning about uptime/SLA expectations during validator outages

capabilities.name: Ledger structure & ledger objects
capabilities.summary: Each ledger version has three parts: a fixed-size header (ledger index, ledger hash, parent hash, close time, state-data hash, transaction-set hash), the transaction set (transactions applied in canonical order, each with metadata describing its effects), and the state data - a tree of ledger entries (ledger objects) each keyed by a unique 256-bit identifier. Ledgers chain by sequential index back to the genesis ledger; identical hashes guarantee identical contents. Builders read state through ledger objects and write state by submitting transactions.
capabilities.key_fields: Ledger object types: AccountRoot, RippleState (trust line), Offer, Escrow, PayChannel, Check, Ticket, SignerList, DepositPreauth, NFTokenPage, NFTokenOffer, AMM, DID, Credential, PermissionedDomain, Oracle, MPTokenIssuance, MPToken, Vault (newer). API: ledger_entry, account_objects, account_info, ledger, ledger_data, ledger_index vs ledger_hash.
capabilities.gotchas: Two identification schemes - ledger_index (sequence) vs ledger_hash (content); always pin to validated for finality. Each owned ledger object increases your account's owner reserve. Ledger object IDs are deterministic keylets (hash of type + fields); some pre-fix entries lacked identifying fields (addressed by fixIncludeKeyletFields). account_objects on a busy account may paginate (marker). NFTs live in NFTokenPage objects, not one-object-per-NFT, which affects reserve math.

capabilities.name: Transaction cost & fee escalation
capabilities.summary: Every transaction destroys a small amount of XRP as its cost (anti-spam, deflationary). The reference/base cost is 10 drops (0.00001 XRP) for a standard transaction. Under load the open-ledger cost escalates exponentially once a soft per-ledger transaction limit is reached, so transactions that don't meet the open-ledger cost but exceed the local load cost get queued for a later ledger. The actual required fee = base_fee * load_factor / load_base, queried live via the fee API method.
capabilities.key_fields: Fee field (in drops, set before signing); reference cost 10 drops; multipliers: SetRegularKey reset = 0 drops, multisigned = 10 * (1 + number of signatures), AccountDelete = 2,000,000 drops (2 XRP), EscrowFinish with fulfillment = 10 * (33 + fulfillment_bytes/16). API: fee (drops.base_fee, drops.open_ledger_fee, queue stats), server_info (load_factor), server_state.
capabilities.gotchas: The Fee is destroyed even if the transaction FAILS (tec/tem/tef results still burn the fee on tec; only certain reject codes avoid inclusion). Hardcoding 10 drops breaks during congestion - always query fee and pad. AccountDelete costs 2 XRP and can only run if the account has no blocking objects and meets a sequence-gap rule. Multisign and EscrowFinish-with-fulfillment cost materially more. Queued transactions can expire or be replaced; manage Sequence/LastLedgerSequence carefully.

best_for.purpose: Reliable transaction submission under load
Batched/high-frequency game economy txns with fee budgeting

capabilities.name: Account & owner reserves
capabilities.summary: Every XRPL account must hold a minimum XRP balance: a base reserve (currently 1 XRP) plus an owner reserve (currently 0.2 XRP) for each ledger object the account owns (trust lines, offers, escrows, NFT offers, checks, payment channels, signer lists, tickets, etc.). Reserved XRP cannot be spent but is freed when the corresponding object is removed. Reserve amounts are set by validator fee voting and have been lowered over time (the 1 XRP / 0.2 XRP levels reflect a reduction from the older 10 XRP / 2 XRP regime).
capabilities.key_fields: reserve_base_xrp (base, ~1 XRP), reserve_inc_xrp / owner reserve (~0.2 XRP per item); total reserve = reserve_base_xrp + (OwnerCount * reserve_inc_xrp); AccountRoot.OwnerCount; API: server_info (validated_ledger.reserve_base_xrp, reserve_inc_xrp), account_info, account_objects. Reserve changes via fee-voting consensus.
capabilities.gotchas: Reserve is denominated in XRP and is locked, not lost - it is reclaimable by deleting objects. Funding a brand-new account requires sending at least the base reserve (1 XRP) or the account is never created. Each trust line, offer, and NFT-offer adds owner reserve; apps that spam offers can lock up a user's XRP. NFTs themselves are batched into NFTokenPages (each page, holding up to 32 NFTs, costs one owner reserve, not per-NFT). Always read live reserve values from server_info - do not hardcode, because fee voting can change them.

capabilities.name: XRP native asset
capabilities.summary: XRP is the XRP Ledger's native asset, created at genesis with a fixed maximum supply of 100 billion. It is the only asset that is not a trust-line/issued token: it needs no issuer, no trust line, and is the unit for fees and reserves. XRP is divisible to 6 decimal places - 1 XRP = 1,000,000 drops, and all protocol amounts for XRP are expressed in integer drops. Supply is slowly deflationary because every transaction destroys its fee; new XRP is never created. Ripple placed 55 billion XRP in escrow in 2017 to make circulating-supply growth predictable.
capabilities.key_fields: 1 XRP = 1,000,000 drops; max supply 100,000,000,000 XRP; XRP amounts in transactions/API are strings of drops (integers), NOT decimal XRP objects; AccountRoot.Balance is in drops; native XRP needs no trust line; used for Fee, reserves, and as bridge/path-payment liquidity.
capabilities.gotchas: The #1 integration bug: confusing drops with XRP - sending 1000000 means 1 XRP, not 1,000,000 XRP. XRP uses integer drops; issued tokens use a different decimal/value format, so amount serialization differs (string of drops vs object with currency/issuer/value). XRP balance can never go below the account reserve. Burned fees are gone forever - there is no fee rebate. Escrowed Ripple XRP is part of total supply but not circulating; do not treat total = circulating.

best_for.purpose: Native settlement / bridge currency in payments
Hard-capped in-game currency or sink via fee burn

capabilities.name: Amendment process (2/3 supermajority, 2-week activation)
capabilities.summary: Protocol changes ship via amendments, which validators vote on at flag ledgers (every 256th ledger). An amendment that holds more than 80% support among trusted validators for two continuous weeks becomes enabled on mainnet automatically; if support drops below threshold the clock resets. Default votes are baked into each rippled/xrpld release and operators can override them. Servers running software that lacks an enabled amendment become amendment-blocked and stop validating until upgraded. This is the gate that makes every other capability in this lane current-or-not.
capabilities.key_fields: Flag ledger = every 256th ledger (~15 min); >80% support for 2 weeks -> enabled; EnableAmendment pseudo-transaction records activation; amendment IDs (sha512half of the amendment name); API: feature, ledger (amendment majorities), Amendments ledger object. Server states: amendment-blocked when behind an enabled amendment.
capabilities.gotchas: Voting threshold is effectively a >80% supermajority sustained for two weeks - not a one-time snapshot; a temporary dip resets the timer. An amendment can be in 'majority' but not yet enabled (still inside its two-week window). The process is also a kill-switch: the original Batch and fixBatchInnerSigs amendments were marked unsupported in rippled 3.1.1 (Feb 2026) after a flaw was found during voting, proving amendments can be pulled before activation. Always verify an amendment's ACTUAL on-chain status (feature method / explorer) - do not assume from version notes.

capabilities.name: rippled / xrpld core server (v3.2.0 rebrand)
capabilities.summary: rippled is the reference C++ server that runs the XRP Ledger: it participates in the peer-to-peer network, runs consensus, validates ledgers, holds ledger state, and serves the full JSON-RPC/WebSocket API including transaction submission. As of v3.2.0 (targeting June 15 2026) the software is being renamed rippled -> xrpld, decoupling the name from Ripple the company and delivering a 30-40% memory-footprint reduction plus rounding/number-handling fixes. Builders submit transactions and query live/consensus data through a rippled/xrpld node (or an upstream provider's node).

capabilities.name: Clio API server (history & read scaling)
capabilities.summary: Clio is a read-optimized API server that extracts validated ledger and transaction data from an upstream rippled/xrpld node (via gRPC) and serves it over the same WebSocket/HTTP API, using ~4x less storage than rippled. It does NOT join the P2P network or participate in consensus. Clio is the standard way to serve historical queries, account_tx, and NFT data at scale: multiple Clio instances can share one Cassandra/ScyllaDB dataset, taking read load off validation nodes. Requests needing live/consensus data are transparently forwarded to the upstream rippled.
capabilities.key_fields: Backed by Cassandra or ScyllaDB; serves account_info, account_tx, account_objects, ledger, tx, nft_info, nft_history, book_offers (read paths); forwards to rippled for: submit, submit_multisigned, fee, ledger_closed, ledger_current, ripple_path_find, manifest, channel_authorize, channel_verify, and ledger_index current/closed or accounts/queue/full flags.
capabilities.gotchas: Clio cannot submit transactions or give you the current (unvalidated) ledger from its own store - those forward to rippled, so a Clio-only deployment without a healthy upstream node degrades. Clio serves VALIDATED data only - great for finality, but it lags the absolute tip by design. NFT-specific methods (nft_info, nft_history) are a Clio strength rippled lacks. Make sure your Clio is fed by a node retaining enough history for your queries, or historical lookups return missing-data errors.

capabilities.name: Batch transactions (BatchV1_1 revival)

It is a powerful primitive for multi-step game/DeFi actions, but its rollout is a cautionary tale: the original Batch and fixBatchInnerSigs amendments were found to contain a critical signature-bypass flaw (discovered Feb 19 2026 by Cantina AI's Apex tooling) while still in validator voting, and were marked unsupported in the emergency rippled 3.1.1 release (Feb 23 2026). capabilities.name: Dynamic NFTs (DynamicNFT / XLS-46)
capabilities.summary: DynamicNFT (XLS-46) extends the native XLS-20 NFT system to allow mutable NFTs: the issuer can update an NFToken's URI field after minting, enabling evolving metadata (game state, leveling, dynamic art) without burning and re-minting. It was enabled on mainnet on 2025-06-11. It sits on top of the already-live XLS-20 native NFT primitives (mint, burn, create/accept/cancel offers, broker mode).
capabilities.key_fields: Transaction: NFTokenModify (update URI); requires the tfMutable flag set at NFTokenMint time; ledger objects: NFTokenPage, NFTokenOffer; base XLS-20 txns: NFTokenMint, NFTokenBurn, NFTokenCreateOffer, NFTokenAcceptOffer, NFTokenCancelOffer. capabilities.gotchas: Only NFTs minted with the mutable flag can be modified - you cannot retroactively make an existing immutable NFT dynamic. Only the URI (metadata pointer) changes; the on-chain token identity is fixed, so off-chain metadata at that URI must be managed carefully (and is only as trustworthy as its hosting). NFTs are stored in NFTokenPages (up to 32 per page) which affects owner-reserve math. For NFT history/queries at scale use Clio's nft_info/nft_history. Confirm DynamicNFT is enabled on the network you target (it is on mainnet).

research.domain: Regulated-issuer rails on XRPL: RLUSD, stablecoin/RWA tokenization, and the on-chain compliance stack (clawback, freeze, authorized trust lines, credentials, permissioned domains/DEX, Multi-Purpose Tokens).
research.notes: Mid-2026 synthesis (verified June 2026). RLUSD (Ripple USD) is LIVE on XRPL mainnet, issued natively as a standard trust-line fungible token from issuer rMxCKbEDwqr76QuheSUMdEGf4B9xJ8m5De / rRLUSD... family (canonical mainnet issuer rQhWct2fv4Vc4KRjRgMrxa8xPN9Zx9iLKV reported by trackers; currency code 524C555344000000000000000000000000000000 = 'RLUSD' as 40-char hex). It launched Dec 2024 and as of mid-2026 sits near ~$1.7-1.8B market cap, but ~80%+ of supply now lives on Ethereum, not XRPL — XRPL is the minority chain by volume despite being a native home. RLUSD's actual XRPL issuer flags: DefaultRipple ON, AllowTrustLineClawback ON, GlobalFreeze capability, DepositAuth ON, DisallowXRP ON, TickSize set — and notably RequireAuth (Authorized Trust Lines) is NOT enabled, so anyone can open an RLUSD trust line without per-account allow-listing. The institutional edge matured fast in 2025-2026: MPTokensV1 (Multi-Purpose Tokens) went live on mainnet Oct 1 2025, giving RWA issuers a native token primitive with built-in supply caps, transfer fees, lock/clawback flags and on-chain metadata — no smart contracts needed. The 'permissioning stack' completed in early 2026: Credentials (XLS-70), Permissioned Domains (XLS-80, live ~Feb 4 2026), and Permissioned DEX (XLS-81) let institutions trade in credential-gated, KYC'd liquidity zones on the public ledger while keeping PII off-chain. Clawback (XLS-39d/73) has been live since Feb 2024 and AMMClawback since Jan 2025. XRPL-hosted RWA crossed ~$2B+ in early 2026 (Ondo OUSG, Archax, Mercado Bitcoin, Guggenheim). The clean mental model: trust-line issued currencies + flags = the proven stablecoin pattern (RLUSD uses it); MPTs = the modern RWA primitive; Credentials/Permissioned Domains/DEX = the compliance gating layer. Builders targeting institutional/payments should prefer MPTs for new RWA issuance and the permissioning stack for regulated venues.

capabilities.name: XRPL stablecoin issuer pattern (trust-line issued currency)
capabilities.summary: The proven, battle-tested pattern for issuing a fiat-backed token on XRPL using native trust-line issued currencies. Three steps: choose a currency code, have holders create trust lines to the issuer, then send Payment transactions up to trust limits. Uses a hot/cold wallet split (cold = issuing address, hot = operational/distribution) for security. This is what RLUSD itself uses.

Each trust line costs the holder an owner reserve in XRP. Decide clawback at issuer genesis (cannot add later). Do NOT trade from the issuing (cold) address — use a separate hot account for DEX/AMM to maintain security boundaries. Issuers should complete Ripple's Token Issuer Self-Assessment Questionnaire for compliance.

capabilities.name: Multi-Purpose Tokens (MPTs)
capabilities.summary: A native, compact fungible-token primitive purpose-built for RWA and institutional issuance — the modern alternative to trust-line tokens. MPTs use a simpler unidirectional model (no rippling, no balance netting), embed supply caps, transfer fees, lock/clawback/auth flags and on-chain metadata directly in the ledger, and require no smart contracts. Each issuance gets a unique 192-bit MPTokenIssuanceID instead of relying on currency codes.
capabilities.key_fields: MPTokenIssuanceCreate / MPTokenAuthorize / MPTokenIssuanceSet / MPTokenIssuanceDestroy transactions; flags lsfMPTCanTransfer, lsfMPTRequireAuth, lsfMPTCanLock, lsfMPTCanClawback, lsfMPTCanEscrow, lsfMPTCanTrade (DEX not yet implemented); MaximumAmount (supply cap), TransferFee (0-50% in 0.0001% increments), AssetScale; on-chain metadata <=1024 bytes (keys: t=ticker, n=name, ac=asset class rwa/defi/gaming, as=subclass stablecoin/treasury/equity/real_estate, in=issuer name, i=icon).
capabilities.gotchas: Issuers cannot hold their own MPTs; returning an MPT to the issuer burns it. lsfMPTCanClawback and the immutable control flags must be chosen at issuance — they cannot be added later (DynamicMPT/XLS-94 to relax some metadata is still in development). MPT DEX trading (CanTrade) is not yet implemented, so MPTs do not yet trade on the native DEX/AMM the way trust-line tokens do — for tradable stablecoins today, trust-line issued currencies remain the path. Metadata is immutable today.

capabilities.name: Token Clawback
capabilities.summary: Lets a token issuer forcibly recover (claw back) issued tokens from a holder's balance — the key compliance lever for sanctioned-address recovery, fraud reversal, and court-ordered seizure. Disabled by default and must be armed before any tokens are issued. Applies to trust-line issued currencies; MPTs have an equivalent CanClawback flag.
capabilities.key_fields: Clawback transaction type; lsfAllowTrustLineClawback flag set via AccountSet (must be set when issuer has no trust lines yet); Amount/holder specified per claw-back; mutually exclusive with lsfNoFreeze considerations.
capabilities.gotchas: Cannot be enabled after the issuer has issued tokens or has trust lines — it is a genesis-time decision. It is mutually exclusive with the No Freeze setting in spirit (an issuer wanting full irreversibility would set NoFreeze and forgo clawback). XRP itself has no issuer and can NEVER be clawed back — clawback only applies to issued tokens. Holders can see the flag, so clawback-armed tokens may be perceived as less trustless; institutions treat it as a feature, retail may not.

capabilities.summary: Extends clawback to tokens that are locked inside Automated Market Maker (AMM) pools, so a clawback-enabled issued token can participate in XRPL's native AMM without creating an un-recoverable gap. Clawing back from an AMM affects the holder's LP position, not other LPs' assets; understand the pool-share mechanics before relying on it for enforcement. This is enabling infrastructure, not something most app builders call directly.

capabilities.name: Authorized Trust Lines (RequireAuth)
capabilities.summary: An allow-listing mechanism: when an issuer sets the Require Auth flag, no account can hold the issuer's token until the issuer explicitly authorizes that account's trust line. This is the strictest on-ledger holder gating for a trust-line stablecoin — used by issuers who need every holder pre-approved (e.g., permissioned securities). RLUSD deliberately does NOT use it.
capabilities.key_fields: lsfRequireAuth flag set via AccountSet (must be set before issuing); TrustSet with tfSetfAuth by the issuer to authorize a specific holder's trust line; combine with DepositAuth for inbound payment gating.
capabilities.gotchas: Must be enabled before issuing any tokens. Creates operational overhead — the issuer must authorize every single trust line, which doesn't scale for open retail distribution (hence RLUSD skips it and relies on clawback/freeze instead). For dynamic, credential-based gating that scales, prefer Permissioned Domains + Credentials over per-trust-line RequireAuth. RequireAuth gates HOLDING; DepositAuth gates RECEIVING payments — they are different controls.

capabilities.name: Token Freeze (individual, global, deep freeze)
capabilities.summary: Issuer controls to halt movement of issued tokens. Individual freeze locks a single holder's trust line; global freeze halts all transfers and DEX trading of the issuer's tokens; deep freeze (DeepFreeze amendment) additionally blocks the holder from sending OR receiving, closing a gap in the original freeze. The No Freeze flag permanently surrenders this power. RLUSD retains freeze authority (NoFreeze off).
capabilities.key_fields: TrustSet with tfSetFreeze / tfSetDeepFreeze for individual lines; lsfGlobalFreeze via AccountSet for global; lsfNoFreeze (irreversible opt-out); DeepFreeze amendment enables the stricter variant.
capabilities.gotchas: lsfNoFreeze is irreversible — once you renounce freeze you can never freeze again (a trust signal to holders, a loss of control for the issuer). Global freeze stops legitimate users too, so it is a break-glass action. Original individual freeze only stopped the holder from SENDING; DeepFreeze was added so a frozen holder also cannot receive — use deep freeze for true holds. XRP cannot be frozen (no issuer).

capabilities.name: Credentials
capabilities.summary: An on-ledger, privacy-preserving attestation primitive: a trusted issuer attaches a verifiable credential (e.g., 'KYC-passed', 'accredited investor') to an account, recording only PROOF of the credential on-chain while personal data stays off-ledger. It is the foundation of the XRPL permissioning stack and a prerequisite for Permissioned Domains.

capabilities.gotchas: Credentials carry only a reference/proof — the actual identity data lives off-chain with the credential issuer; you must trust that issuer. Permissioned Domains require Credentials to be enabled; PermissionedDomainSet transactions are invalid without it. A credential is only as good as its issuer's vetting and revocation discipline — design for expiration and revocation.

capabilities.name: Permissioned Domains
capabilities.summary: Credential-gated zones on the public XRPL. A domain operator defines which credentials are accepted; any account holding a valid accepted credential automatically becomes a member. This lets institutions apply KYC/sanctions constraints to activity (e.g., who may participate in a liquidity venue) without forking the chain or moving off the public ledger.

capabilities.gotchas: Requires Credentials to be active — a domain references credential types, so the credential layer must exist first. Membership is dynamic: it follows credential validity, so revoking/expiring a credential changes membership. Activated on mainnet ~Feb 4 2026 after >91% validator support — relatively new, so tooling and ecosystem adoption are still maturing. Domains gate eligibility; they do not themselves move or custody assets.

research.domain: Fungible token issuance on the XRP Ledger — trust-line IOUs and Multi-Purpose Tokens (MPTs)
research.notes: As of mid-2026 the XRPL has two distinct native fungible-token models. The legacy model is trust-line IOUs: bidirectional credit relationships (RippleState entries) created via TrustSet, governed by rippling/NoRipple, RequireAuth allow-listing, TransferRate fees, and a freeze suite (individual, global, NoFreeze, and DeepFreeze which landed on mainnet 2025-05-05). Clawback for IOUs went live 2024-02-08; AMMClawback followed. The newer model is Multi-Purpose Tokens (XLS-33), enabled by the MPTokensV1 amendment on mainnet ~2025-10-01 — a unidirectional, fixed-precision, single-ledger-object token with on-chain JSON metadata and per-issuance capability flags (CanTransfer, RequireAuth, CanLock, CanClawback, CanEscrow, CanTrade). MPTs are the recommended path for new RWA/stablecoin issuance because of cleaner compliance controls and far lower reserve/relationship overhead than trust lines; the trade-off in mid-2026 is that MPT DEX/AMM trading is still maturing (MPTokensV2 in development, lsfMPTCanTrade not yet implemented). Token Escrow (2025-02-12) extended escrow to both IOUs and MPTs. Decision rule: choose MPTs for new issuances needing native metadata, supply caps, and per-issuance controls without trust-line management; choose IOUs when you need full DEX/AMM liquidity today, pathfinding/rippling, or existing-ecosystem interop. XRP itself is never an issued token — it cannot be frozen, clawed back, or carry a transfer fee.

capabilities.name: Issued Currencies (IOUs) & Trust Lines
capabilities.summary: Issued currencies (IOUs) are tokens represented as balances on bidirectional trust lines between an issuer and a holder, stored as RippleState ledger entries. A holder opens or modifies a trust line with a TrustSet transaction declaring a currency code, issuer, and credit limit. This is the original XRPL fungible-token model and underpins stablecoins, fiat representations, and most DEX/AMM liquidity. Each trust line consumes an owner reserve, so issuers and holders must budget XRP reserves.
capabilities.key_fields: TrustSet: LimitAmount {currency, issuer, value}, Flags (tfSetNoRipple, tfSetfAuth, tfSetFreeze). RippleState: Balance, LowLimit, HighLimit, HighNode/LowNode, Flags. Currency codes: 3-char standard or 40-char hex. Owner reserve per trust line.
capabilities.gotchas: Each trust line costs an owner reserve in XRP for the account holding it; mass distribution scales reserve cost. Balances net bidirectionally and can ripple between holders of the same issuer unless NoRipple is set. A trust line with limit 0 and zero balance can be deleted to reclaim reserve. Currency 'XRP' is reserved/invalid as an issued code.

capabilities.name: TrustSet Transaction
capabilities.summary: TrustSet creates or modifies a trust line linking two accounts for a specific issued currency. Holders use it to declare a credit limit (LimitAmount) toward an issuer; issuers use it to authorize trust lines (with tfSetfAuth) and to set per-line flags such as NoRipple and Freeze. It is the single transaction that drives nearly all IOU lifecycle operations from the relationship side.
capabilities.key_fields: LimitAmount {currency, issuer, value}; Flags: tfSetfAuth, tfSetNoRipple/tfClearNoRipple, tfSetFreeze/tfClearFreeze, tfSetDeepFreeze/tfClearDeepFreeze; QualityIn, QualityOut.
capabilities.gotchas: tfSetfAuth can only be set by the issuer and cannot be cleared once set. Setting a trust line authorization (RequireAuth flow) requires submitting TrustSet from the issuing address with the holder as the issuer of LimitAmount and value 0. Deep freeze flags require the standard freeze to already be in place. Quality fields (QualityIn/QualityOut) affect exchange rates and are easy to misconfigure.

capabilities.name: Rippling, NoRipple & Default Ripple
capabilities.summary: Rippling is atomic net settlement of balances among parties who hold the same issuer's currency, letting one holder pay another with the issuer as a passive intermediary. The No Ripple flag (set per trust line via TrustSet tfSetNoRipple) prevents a line from rippling. The account-level Default Ripple setting determines the default NoRipple state for new trust lines: when Default Ripple is disabled (the account default), new lines default to NoRipple enabled.
capabilities.key_fields: TrustSet flags tfSetNoRipple / tfClearNoRipple; trust-line flag lsfNoRipple (lsfLowNoRipple/lsfHighNoRipple); AccountSet asfDefaultRipple flag; account flag lsfDefaultRipple.
capabilities.gotchas: Issuers MUST enable Default Ripple so that holders can pay each other through them — without it, the issuer's own lines block rippling and the token does not circulate. Conversely, ordinary users and operational/treasury wallets should keep NoRipple set to avoid unwanted value flowing across their lines. NoRipple only has an effect when set on BOTH sides relevant to a path. This is a top source of 'why won't my token move' bugs.

capabilities.name: Token Freeze (Individual, Global, NoFreeze)
capabilities.summary: Issuers of trust-line tokens can freeze balances for compliance and incident response. Individual Freeze restricts one counterparty on one trust line; Global Freeze freezes all of an issuer's lines at once; NoFreeze is a permanent, irreversible surrender of the issuer's freeze power (master-key only). A frozen counterparty cannot decrease its balance except by paying the issuer directly, and its sell offers become unfunded.
capabilities.key_fields: TrustSet tfSetFreeze/tfClearFreeze (individual); AccountSet asfGlobalFreeze (global); AccountSet asfNoFreeze (permanent, master key only); trust-line flags lsfLowFreeze/lsfHighFreeze; account flags lsfGlobalFreeze/lsfNoFreeze.
capabilities.gotchas: XRP cannot be frozen — freeze applies only to issued tokens. NoFreeze is irreversible and can only be set with the master key (not regular/regular-key or multisig); once set the issuer keeps Global Freeze but can never disable it again. Standard (individual/global) freeze still lets a holder RECEIVE the token — use Deep Freeze to block incoming as well. Freezing is a centralization signal that markets and exchanges may scrutinize.

capabilities.name: Deep Freeze
capabilities.summary: Deep Freeze extends individual trust-line freeze so a frozen holder can no longer RECEIVE the token either — closing the gap where standard freeze still allowed incoming balance. The deep-frozen counterparty cannot increase or decrease its balance except in direct payments to the issuer, and can only send the currency directly to the issuer. It affects payments, offers, the DEX, and AMM interactions. The issuer must apply a standard freeze before enacting a deep freeze.
capabilities.key_fields: TrustSet tfSetDeepFreeze / tfClearDeepFreeze; trust-line flags lsfLowDeepFreeze / lsfHighDeepFreeze. Requires prior standard freeze on the same line.
capabilities.gotchas: You cannot deep-freeze a line that is not already standard-frozen, and you must clear deep freeze before clearing the standard freeze. Applies to issued tokens only (not XRP). Reaches into DEX/AMM so deep-frozen balances become fully inert for trading — useful for hard compliance holds but blunt for ordinary disputes.

capabilities.name: Clawback (Issued Currencies)
capabilities.summary: Clawback lets a token issuer recover (claw back) issued currency from a holder's trust line via a Clawback transaction — essential for compliance scenarios like recovering tokens sent to a sanctioned or compromised account. It is opt-in and irreversible to enable: the issuer must set the Allow Trustline Clawback flag (AccountSet asfAllowTrustLineClawback) BEFORE issuing any tokens, and that account can then never use NoFreeze, and vice versa.
capabilities.key_fields: Clawback transaction: Amount {currency, issuer (the holder being clawed), value}; AccountSet asfAllowTrustLineClawback (must be enabled pre-issuance); account flag lsfAllowTrustLineClawback. Cannot be used on XRP.
capabilities.gotchas: Allow Trustline Clawback must be enabled before the account issues ANY token — you cannot retrofit it onto an existing issuer that already distributed. It is mutually exclusive with NoFreeze. In the Clawback transaction the Amount.issuer field names the HOLDER (counterparty) you're clawing from, which trips up newcomers. XRP cannot be clawed back. AMMClawback (separate, enabled) is required to claw tokens that holders deposited into an AMM.

capabilities.name: Transfer Fees (TransferRate)
capabilities.summary: Issuers of trust-line tokens can charge a transfer fee when holders move the token among themselves. The fee is set via the account-level TransferRate field; the sender pays extra and the recipient gets the intended amount, with the difference burned (reducing the issuer's outstanding obligations). Fees do not apply when sending directly to or from the issuing account.
capabilities.key_fields: AccountSet TransferRate: integer where 1000000000 = 0% (no fee) up to 2000000000 = 100%; e.g. 1005000000 = 0.5%; value 0 also means no fee. Precision to 0.0000001%.
capabilities.gotchas: TransferRate is set on the ISSUER account and applies to all of that issuer's tokens. The issuing address is exempt, but separate operational/treasury addresses are NOT — payments through them incur the fee. In multi-hop rippling paths the fee compounds at each intermediary, so senders must compute send amounts backward from the recipient. MPTs have their own per-issuance transfer fee field (0–50%) — distinct from this account-level TransferRate.

capabilities.name: Authorized Trust Lines (RequireAuth)
capabilities.summary: An issuer can set the RequireAuth flag so that no holder can hold its tokens until the issuer explicitly authorizes that holder's trust line — an allow-list / KYC gate at the protocol level. After RequireAuth is set, the issuer authorizes a line by sending a TrustSet from the issuing address naming the holder, value 0, with the tfSetfAuth flag.
capabilities.key_fields: AccountSet asfRequireAuth (must be set before issuing); account flag lsfRequireAuth; TrustSet tfSetfAuth (issuer-only, cannot be cleared); trust-line flags lsfLowAuth/lsfHighAuth.
capabilities.gotchas: RequireAuth must be enabled before the account issues any tokens. Authorization is one-way: tfSetfAuth cannot be cleared once granted (revocation is done via freeze/clawback, not de-authorization). Every new holder requires an issuer transaction, which adds operational overhead for large user bases — consider MPT RequireAuth instead for new projects.

capabilities.name: Multi-Purpose Tokens (MPTs)
capabilities.summary: Multi-Purpose Tokens (XLS-33) are a native XRPL fungible-token type optimized for stablecoins and real-world assets, enabled on mainnet by the MPTokensV1 amendment around 2025-10-01. Unlike trust-line IOUs, an MPT is a single MPTokenIssuance ledger object identified by a 192-bit MPT Issuance ID, is unidirectional (clean holder/issuer separation, no balance netting, no rippling), uses fixed-precision integers, carries on-chain JSON metadata, and exposes per-issuance capability flags. It dramatically reduces the relationship/reserve overhead of mass token distribution.
capabilities.key_fields: MPTIssuanceID (192-bit); on-chain metadata (up to 1024 bytes JSON: ticker, name, icon URI, asset class/subclass, issuer name, URIs); MaximumAmount (supply cap); TransferFee (0–50%, 0.0001% increments, burned); AssetScale; issuance flags lsfMPTCanTransfer, lsfMPTRequireAuth, lsfMPTCanLock, lsfMPTCanClawback, lsfMPTCanEscrow, lsfMPTCanTrade.
capabilities.gotchas: Capability flags are mostly FIXED at issuance and cannot be added later in V1 — decide CanTransfer/CanClawback/CanLock/RequireAuth up front (DynamicMPT, in development, will relax some of this). Without lsfMPTCanTransfer the token is non-transferable (holder<->issuer only). lsfMPTCanTrade exists but DEX/AMM trading of MPTs is not yet implemented in V1 (MPTokensV2 in development). MaximumAmount is a hard cap. MPTs and IOUs are separate systems — an MPT is not interchangeable with a same-named IOU.

capabilities.name: IOU vs MPT — Decision Guide
capabilities.summary: Choosing between trust-line IOUs and MPTs is the central token decision in mid-2026. Pick MPTs for NEW issuances that want native on-chain metadata, a hard supply cap, bundled per-issuance controls (auth/lock/clawback), and low reserve/relationship overhead for many holders — the recommended default for fresh stablecoin/RWA projects. Pick IOUs when you need deep DEX/AMM liquidity and pathfinding/rippling TODAY, interop with the large existing token ecosystem, or arbitrary decimal precision, since MPT DEX/AMM support is still maturing (MPTokensV2 in development).
capabilities.key_fields: Decision axes: liquidity needs (DEX/AMM today -> IOU), holder scale & reserve cost (large -> MPT), need for on-chain metadata/supply cap (-> MPT), need for mutable controls later (-> IOU now, watch DynamicMPT), rippling/pathfinding (-> IOU), precision (arbitrary decimals -> IOU, fixed integer+scale -> MPT).
capabilities.gotchas: MPT capability flags are immutable in V1 — mis-scoping at mint is unrecoverable; IOU controls are more retrofittable but with their own pre-issuance gotchas (clawback/RequireAuth must precede issuance). MPTs cannot yet be traded on the native DEX/AMM in V1. Do not assume an IOU and a same-named MPT are interchangeable — they are separate ledger systems. Neither model applies to XRP, which carries no issuer controls at all.

research.notes: Mid-2026 synthesis (verified against xrpl.org, XRPLF GitHub, and rippled release notes). The stable, mainnet-live core is rock solid: the common transaction model (Account/Sequence/Fee/Flags/Memos/SourceTag/DestinationTag), the autofill->sign->submit->verify reliable-submission lifecycle, the tes/tec/tef/tem/tel/ter result taxonomy, Tickets (TicketBatch amendment), multisign (MultiSign + MultiSignReserve), AccountSet flags, SetRegularKey, and AccountDelete (DeletableAccounts) are all enabled and battle-tested. The two MUCH-hyped new primitives are NOT mainnet-enabled as of mid-2026 and a builder must NOT assume they are: (1) Batch (XLS-56) was caught with a critical inner-transaction signature-bypass flaw on 2026-02-19 (Cantina AI 'Apex' + Pranamya Keshkamat, ~$80B at theoretical risk), never reached mainnet, and was marked unsupported in rippled 3.1.1 (2026-02-23) along with fixBatchInnerSigs; a corrected BatchV1_1 is implemented but still under review with no release date. (2) Permission Delegation (XLS-75 / DelegateSet + Delegate ledger entry) had a fee-charging-to-arbitrary-accounts bug reported 2025-09-15 (tequ), was disabled in rippled 2.6.1, and a replacement PermissionDelegationV1_1 (superseding the old PermissionDelegation + DelegateV1_1) plus fixDelegateV1_1 are code-complete-ish but not yet open for voting as of late 2025/2026. Latest rippled at synthesis time is 3.1.3 (2026-05-14, fixCleanup3_1_3). Bottom line for builders: design against the stable core today; treat Batch and Delegation as testnet/devnet-only and re-check known-amendments before relying on them.

capabilities.name: Transaction Common Fields
capabilities.summary: Every XRPL transaction shares a common field set regardless of TransactionType: Account (sender address), TransactionType, Fee (drops destroyed), Sequence (must be exactly account's next number), and optional Flags, Memos, SourceTag, LastLedgerSequence, AccountTxnID, NetworkID, Signers, SigningPubKey, TxnSignature, TicketSequence, and Delegate. These fields are the foundation of all account interaction; understanding them correctly is prerequisite to building anything. Many fields (SigningPubKey, TxnSignature) are added during signing; others (Fee, Sequence, LastLedgerSequence) are typically autofilled.
capabilities.key_fields: Account (sender); TransactionType; Fee (integer drops); Sequence (exactly account's next, or 0 when using TicketSequence); Flags (bitwise, type-specific + global tfFullyCanonicalSig 0x80000000 deprecated under RequireFullyCanonicalSig); Memos (array of {Memo:{MemoData,MemoType,MemoFormat}} hex, ~1KB cap); SourceTag (uint32); LastLedgerSequence (expiry ledger); AccountTxnID (chain to prior tx hash); NetworkID (required on networks id>=1025, replay protection); SigningPubKey/TxnSignature (auto on sign); TicketSequence; Delegate (sender-on-behalf-of, pays fee).
capabilities.gotchas: Sequence must be EXACTLY one greater than the account's last applied sequence — gaps stall all later transactions. Memos must be hex-encoded; the ~1KB total cap is easy to exceed. DestinationTag/SourceTag are NOT enforced unless the receiving account sets asfRequireDest — never assume tag routing is mandatory. tfFullyCanonicalSig is now a no-op (deprecated). NetworkID is mandatory on sidechains/custom networks (id>=1025) but must be omitted on mainnet (id 0).

best_for.purpose: Constructing any valid transaction
Tagging payments to exchange/hosted subaccounts
Attaching on-chain metadata to game/asset events

capabilities.name: Reliable Transaction Submission Lifecycle (autofill -> sign -> submit -> verify)
capabilities.summary: The canonical four-phase pattern for getting a transaction onto a validated ledger safely. Autofill populates Fee (from current load), Sequence (from account_info), and LastLedgerSequence (last validated + a small buffer). Sign locally (secret never touches the network), producing SigningPubKey + TxnSignature + the tx hash. Submit returns only a PROVISIONAL result. Verify by polling the tx by hash until validated:true, or treat the tx as permanently failed once LastLedgerSequence passes without inclusion. This pattern is the difference between idempotent, recoverable payment systems and double-spend/limbo bugs.
capabilities.key_fields: Autofill: Fee, Sequence, LastLedgerSequence (set to last validated ledger + ~4). Sign: SigningPubKey, TxnSignature, computed tx hash. Submit: provisional engine_result (NOT final). Verify: tx method by hash, check validated:true; persist hash+Sequence+LastLedgerSequence BEFORE submit for crash recovery.
capabilities.gotchas: A success engine_result from submit means 'received', NOT 'applied to a validated ledger' — never confirm a payment on the provisional result. Without LastLedgerSequence a stuck tx can be applied much later (limbo). The Sequence number provides at-most-once semantics: re-signing the same Sequence after the original validated produces a tefPAST_SEQ, not a double-spend — but you MUST persist the hash to know which happened. tesSUCCESS and tec are only final in a validated ledger.

best_for.purpose: Production payment dispatch with retry safety
Idempotent in-game economy transactions
Recoverable minting/transfer pipelines

sources.title: Reliable Transaction Submission
sources.claim: Prescribes autofilling Fee/Sequence/LastLedgerSequence, local signing, persisting before submit, and polling for validated:true since submit results are only provisional.

capabilities.name: Transaction Results & Metadata (tes / tec / tef / tem / tel / ter)
capabilities.summary: XRPL result codes carry meaning in their three-letter prefix and only become final inside a validated ledger. tesSUCCESS = applied successfully. tec = failed to achieve its purpose BUT was included and the fee was destroyed (claimed cost). tef = cannot apply now or ever (e.g. already applied, tefPAST_SEQ, tefMAX_LEDGER). tem = malformed (bad syntax/signature, never valid). tel = local server condition (e.g. load); ter = retryable, may succeed in a later ledger. Transaction metadata (AffectedNodes, delivered_amount) describes the exact ledger-state changes — read delivered_amount, never Amount, to know what actually moved.
capabilities.key_fields: tesSUCCESS (applied); tec* (included, fee burned, goal not met — e.g. tecUNFUNDED, tecNO_DST, tecPATH_DRY); tef* (final failure — tefPAST_SEQ, tefMAX_LEDGER, tefALREADY); tem* (malformed — temMALFORMED, temBAD_SIGNATURE); tel* (local — telINSUF_FEE_P); ter* (retryable — terQUEUED, terPRE_SEQ). Metadata: AffectedNodes (Created/Modified/Deleted ledger entries), TransactionResult, delivered_amount.
capabilities.gotchas: A tec result STILL costs the fee and STILL increments the Sequence — it occupies a ledger slot, so do not blindly resubmit the same Sequence. Only validated-ledger results are final; a provisional tesSUCCESS can still be replaced. Always use delivered_amount (handles partial payments) instead of the requested Amount. terQUEUED means the tx is in the server queue, not yet applied — keep tracking it.

best_for.purpose: Correctly classifying success vs retry vs permanent failure
Reading actual delivered amounts for accounting
Driving game-economy state from validated ledger metadata

sources.title: Transaction Results

capabilities.name: Account Sequence & Fee Model
capabilities.summary: Each account has a strictly incrementing Sequence number; a transaction is valid only when Sequence is exactly the account's next number (unless it uses a Ticket). The Fee is an integer of XRP drops destroyed (not paid to anyone) — a base minimum (~10 drops on a healthy network) scaled up under load and by transaction type (multisign and special transactions cost more). This deflationary, ordered model gives XRPL its at-most-once execution guarantee and spam resistance. Builders must serialize transactions per account or use Tickets/Batch to parallelize.
capabilities.key_fields: Sequence (uint32, strictly +1 per applied tx); Fee (drops, integer, destroyed); base fee scales with server load (open-ledger cost) and tx type; multisign fee = base x (1 + number of signatures); reference reserves: 1 XRP base account reserve, 0.2 XRP per owned object (owner reserve) as of mid-2026.
capabilities.gotchas: Sending two transactions with the same Sequence makes the second a tefPAST_SEQ once the first validates — to send many txs fast you must pre-assign distinct Sequences (and risk a gap stalling everything) or use Tickets. Fee is BURNED, never refunded, even on tec failures. Under network load the autofilled fee can spike sharply; cap it in code to avoid overpaying. A single stuck low Sequence blocks every higher-Sequence transaction from the same account.

best_for.purpose: Designing per-account transaction serialization
Fee budgeting for high-volume game economies
Batch/parallel issuance planning

sources.title: Transaction Common Fields (Sequence & Fee)
sources.claim: States Sequence must be exactly one greater than the account's previous transaction and Fee is an integer amount of XRP in drops destroyed as the cost of distributing the transaction.

capabilities.name: Tickets (TicketCreate / TicketSequence)
capabilities.summary: Tickets let an account reserve specific sequence numbers ahead of time so transactions can be sent out of order or in parallel. A TicketCreate reserves N sequence numbers (advancing the account Sequence past them); later you submit a transaction with Sequence 0 and TicketSequence set to a reserved number. This solves multi-party signing collected over time, parallel dispatch from a shared account, and pre-authorizing future actions without knowing the live sequence. Each Ticket is one-use and costs 0.2 XRP owner reserve until consumed.
capabilities.key_fields: TicketCreate.TicketCount (how many to reserve); resulting Ticket ledger entries; on use: set Sequence=0 and TicketSequence=<reserved number>; max 250 outstanding Tickets per account; 0.2 XRP owner reserve per outstanding Ticket (released on use); within a ledger, Ticketed txs execute after regular-sequence txs, ordered low->high TicketSequence.
capabilities.gotchas: A Ticket is single-use — it is consumed (removed from the ledger) whether the transaction succeeds or fails with tec. Creating Tickets immediately bumps your account Sequence past all of them, so don't mix that up with normal sequencing. The 250-outstanding cap and 0.2 XRP per-ticket reserve limit how many you can pre-stage. Required the TicketBatch amendment (now long enabled on mainnet).

best_for.purpose: Parallel/out-of-order dispatch from one account
Pre-staging transactions for slow multisign collection
Avoiding sequence-gap stalls in busy services

sources.title: Tickets
sources.claim: Tickets reserve sequence numbers for later use (max 250, 0.2 XRP reserve each), enabling out-of-order transactions via the TicketSequence field; requires the now-active TicketBatch amendment.

capabilities.name: Multisigning (SignerListSet)
capabilities.summary: SignerListSet attaches a list of authorized signers (1-32 entries, each with a SignerWeight) plus a SignerQuorum threshold to an account, enabling M-of-N multisignature control. A transaction is then authorized by collecting enough signatures whose combined weight meets the quorum, supplied in the Signers array. This is the production pattern for treasury accounts, DAOs, and shared studio/wallet control. The MultiSignReserve amendment cut the owner-reserve cost of a signer list to a flat amount instead of scaling per signer.
capabilities.key_fields: SignerListSet.SignerQuorum (min combined weight; 0 = delete list); SignerEntries[] of {Account, SignerWeight}; 1-32 signers, no duplicates, sender cannot list itself; SignerListID (currently only 0 supported); delete by SignerQuorum=0 AND omitting SignerEntries; multisign fee = base x (1 + number of signatures included).
capabilities.gotchas: To delete a signer list you must set SignerQuorum=0 AND omit SignerEntries — doing only one gives temMALFORMED. The submitting account may not appear in its own SignerList. Quorum cannot exceed the sum of weights or the tx fails. Multisigned transactions cost MORE (fee multiplied per included signature) — budget for it. Pre-MultiSignReserve lists carry a higher legacy owner reserve; recreate them to benefit from the lower flat reserve. Pair with asfDisableMaster to make multisign the sole control path.

best_for.purpose: Treasury / shared-control wallets
Studio/org governance over an issuing account
Custody of game-economy reserve accounts

sources.title: SignerListSet
sources.claim: SignerListSet sets a 1-32 entry signer list with per-signer weights and a SignerQuorum (0 deletes the list), enabling multisignature authorization; requires the MultiSign amendment with reserve improved by MultiSignReserve.

capabilities.name: AccountSet Flags
capabilities.summary: AccountSet configures persistent account-level options via SetFlag/ClearFlag (one asf flag per transaction) and a handful of legacy tf flags. These flags control security and economic policy: requiring destination tags, requiring trustline authorization, disabling the master key, default rippling, deposit authorization, freeze controls, clawback opt-in, blocking unwanted incoming objects, and authorizing an NFT minter. AccountSet is the primary lever for hardening and shaping an account before it issues tokens or receives funds.
capabilities.key_fields: SetFlag/ClearFlag take ONE asf value: asfRequireDest(1), asfRequireAuth(2), asfDisallowXRP(3, advisory), asfDisableMaster(4), asfAccountTxnID(5), asfNoFreeze(6, irreversible), asfGlobalFreeze(7), asfDefaultRipple(8), asfDepositAuth(9), asfAuthorizedNFTokenMinter(10), asfDisallowIncomingNFTokenOffer(12), asfDisallowIncomingCheck(13), asfDisallowIncomingPayChan(14), asfDisallowIncomingTrustline(15), asfAllowTrustLineClawback(16), asfAllowTrustLineLocking(17). Also Domain, EmailHash, MessageKey, TransferRate, TickSize, NFTokenMinter, RegularKey fields.
capabilities.gotchas: asfNoFreeze and (effectively) clawback decisions are IRREVERSIBLE — asfNoFreeze permanently surrenders freeze ability, and asfAllowTrustLineClawback can only be set on an account with no existing trustlines/balances. asfDisallowXRP is advisory only — it does NOT actually block XRP at the protocol level, only signals client UIs. asfRequireAuth must be set BEFORE issuing tokens. Only one asf flag changes per AccountSet; the legacy tf flags (tfRequireDestTag etc.) are being phased out in favor of asf. Setting asfDisableMaster without a working regular key or signer list locks you out.

best_for.purpose: Hardening an issuing/treasury account
Configuring token issuance policy (auth, rippling, clawback)
Authorizing a delegated NFT minter

sources.title: AccountSet
sources.claim: AccountSet enables/disables account options via SetFlag/ClearFlag using asf flags (asfRequireDest, asfRequireAuth, asfDisableMaster, asfNoFreeze, asfDefaultRipple, asfDepositAuth, asfAllowTrustLineClawback, etc.).

capabilities.name: SetRegularKey (Regular Key Pair)
capabilities.summary: SetRegularKey assigns (or removes) a secondary key pair that can sign transactions for the account in place of the master key. This is the standard XRPL key-rotation and hot/cold separation primitive: keep the master key offline, sign day-to-day with the regular key, and rotate the regular key if it is compromised without losing the account. Combined with asfDisableMaster it lets you fully retire the master key in favor of a rotatable regular key or a signer list.
capabilities.key_fields: SetRegularKey.RegularKey (the new authorized address; omit the field to remove the regular key). The regular key can sign anything the master can EXCEPT it cannot, by itself, re-enable a disabled master in all configurations — plan recovery carefully. Works alongside multisign and (when enabled) delegation.
capabilities.gotchas: If you set asfDisableMaster and your regular key is later lost or compromised with no signer-list fallback, the account can become permanently uncontrollable — always keep a recovery path (signer list or recoverable master). The regular key is a single key; for M-of-N control use SignerListSet instead. Removing the regular key (omit RegularKey) while the master is disabled is a lockout trap.

best_for.purpose: Hot/cold key separation for issuing accounts
Rotating compromised signing keys without account loss
Securing automated game-economy service accounts

sources.title: Transaction Common Fields / Cryptographic Keys (SigningPubKey)
sources.claim: Transactions are authorized by the account's master, regular, or signer-list keys; SigningPubKey identifies which key signed, supporting regular-key rotation set via SetRegularKey.

capabilities.name: AccountDelete
capabilities.summary: AccountDelete removes an account from the ledger and sends its leftover XRP to a Destination account, partially recovering the base reserve. It is heavily gated: the account's Sequence + 256 must be below the current ledger index (replay protection), the account must own no blocking objects (escrows, checks, payment channels, RippleState trustlines with balance, NFTs, Offers above the threshold, etc.), and the Destination must be funded. It costs a special high fee equal to the owner reserve (0.2 XRP), destroyed not refunded, to discourage churn.
capabilities.key_fields: AccountDelete.Destination (recipient of remaining XRP, must be funded, cannot be self); optional DestinationTag; Fee = special high cost, at least the owner reserve (0.2 XRP), destroyed; precondition: account Sequence + 256 < current ledger index; blocking objects prevent deletion (escrows, checks, paychannels, trustlines with balance, NFTs, signer lists do NOT block, etc.).
capabilities.gotchas: You CANNOT delete an account that owns blocking ledger objects — you must first delete/resolve every escrow, check, payment channel, NFT, and non-zero trustline. The Sequence+256 rule means a freshly funded account cannot be deleted until 256 ledgers pass. The 0.2 XRP deletion fee is DESTROYED, so deletion never fully recovers the account's cost (anti-spam by design). If the Destination requires deposit auth, the sender must be preauthorized or it fails. Requires the DeletableAccounts amendment (enabled).

best_for.purpose: Reclaiming reserve from retired service/subaccounts
Account lifecycle cleanup in compliance flows

sources.title: AccountDelete
sources.claim: AccountDelete removes an account (requires DeletableAccounts amendment), costs a special fee of at least the 0.2 XRP owner reserve, requires Sequence+256 below the current ledger, no blocking objects, and a funded Destination for leftover XRP.

capabilities.name: Batch Transactions (XLS-56)
capabilities.summary: Batch (XLS-56) bundles up to 8 inner transactions into one atomic outer transaction with one of four execution modes: tfAllOrNothing (all succeed or none), tfOnlyOne (first success wins), tfUntilFailure (apply in order until one fails), tfIndependent (apply each regardless). Inner transactions are unsigned with zero fee and flagged tfInnerBatchTxn; the outer transaction carries the signatures (including BatchSigners for multi-account atomic trades) and the total fee. CRITICAL: as of mid-2026 Batch is NOT mainnet-enabled — a signature-bypass flaw was caught 2026-02-19 and the amendment was marked unsupported in rippled 3.1.1; a corrected BatchV1_1 is under review with no release date.
capabilities.key_fields: Outer Batch: Flags = exactly one of tfAllOrNothing / tfOnlyOne / tfUntilFailure / tfIndependent; RawTransactions[] (the inner txs); BatchSigners[] for atomic multi-account batches. Inner txs: Fee 0, no SigningPubKey/TxnSignature, Flags include tfInnerBatchTxn (0x40000000), Sequence/TicketSequence assigned by outer context. Max 8 inner. Fee approx = base x 2 + sum(inner fees) + base per extra signature.
capabilities.gotchas: DO NOT build production mainnet flows assuming Batch exists — it is disabled on mainnet as of mid-2026 (rippled 3.1.1 marked Batch and fixBatchInnerSigs unsupported after a critical inner-transaction signature-bypass flaw, ~$80B theoretical risk, caught by Cantina AI 'Apex' + Pranamya Keshkamat on 2026-02-19). The replacement BatchV1_1 is implemented but still under review with no announced date. tfInnerBatchTxn is rejected on normal (non-inner) transactions. Exactly one mode flag must be set. Re-check known-amendments before any reliance; treat as testnet/devnet-only today.

best_for.purpose: Atomic platform-fee + action bundling (when enabled)
Combined NFT mint + offer in one atomic unit (when enabled)
Trustless multi-account swaps (when enabled)

sources.title: Introducing Batch Transactions on the XRP Ledger (XLS-56)
sources.claim: Defines the four Batch modes (AllOrNothing, OnlyOne, UntilFailure, Independent), up to 8 unsigned zero-fee inner transactions, and BatchSigners for multi-account atomic batches.

capabilities.name: Account Permission Delegation (DelegateSet / Delegate)
capabilities.summary: Permission Delegation (XLS-75) lets an account grant another account (the delegate) the right to send specific transaction types or granular permissions on its behalf, via a DelegateSet transaction that writes a Delegate ledger entry. Delegated transactions carry a Delegate common field; the delegate pays the fee from its own balance. Security-critical permissions cannot be delegated. CRITICAL: as of mid-2026 this is NOT mainnet-enabled — a bug allowing fees to be charged to arbitrary accounts (reported 2025-09-15) led to the PermissionDelegation amendment being disabled in rippled 2.6.1; PermissionDelegationV1_1 (superseding the old amendment and DelegateV1_1) plus fixDelegateV1_1 are code-complete-ish but not yet open for voting.
capabilities.key_fields: DelegateSet.Authorize (the delegate account); Permissions[] up to 10 (transaction-type or granular permissions); full-replacement semantics (omitted permissions are revoked; empty array deletes the Delegate entry). Delegated send: set the Delegate common field to the granting account; the delegate signs and pays the fee. Security-sensitive permissions (e.g. account-security operations) are non-delegatable. For >10 permissions, use multisigning instead.
capabilities.gotchas: DO NOT assume delegation works on mainnet as of mid-2026 — the original PermissionDelegation amendment was disabled in rippled 2.6.1 after a fee-charging-to-arbitrary-accounts bug (reported 2025-09-15 by tequ on devnet); the fixed PermissionDelegationV1_1 (which replaces both PermissionDelegation and DelegateV1_1) and fixDelegateV1_1 were not yet open for voting as of late 2025/2026. DelegateSet is full-replacement, not incremental — re-list every permission you want to keep or it is revoked. Max 10 permissions. Re-check known-amendments before relying on it; treat as testnet/devnet-only today.

best_for.purpose: Granting a service narrow send rights without the key (when enabled)
Automated agents acting for a treasury (when enabled)
Delegated game-economy bot permissions (when enabled)

sources.title: Vulnerability Disclosure Report: XRPL Permission Delegation
sources.claim: A bug (reported 2025-09-15) let an account charge transaction fees to any other account; the PermissionDelegation amendment was never enabled on mainnet and was disabled in rippled 2.6.1, with PermissionDelegationV1_1 planned as the fix.

sources.title: DelegateSet
sources.claim: DelegateSet grants a delegate (Authorize) up to 10 transaction-type or granular permissions via full-replacement semantics, with non-delegatable security-critical permissions; requires the PermissionDelegation amendment.

capabilities.name: Source & Destination Tags
capabilities.summary: SourceTag and DestinationTag are optional 32-bit integers that route a transaction to a specific subaccount or context within a hosted/shared XRPL address — the backbone of how exchanges and custodial services map one on-chain address to many users. DestinationTag identifies the recipient subaccount; SourceTag identifies the sender's context for refunds/replies. An account can require a destination tag by setting asfRequireDest, which rejects untagged incoming payments.
capabilities.key_fields: DestinationTag (uint32, routes to recipient subaccount); SourceTag (uint32, sender context); asfRequireDest (AccountSet flag) enforces that incoming payments include a DestinationTag (else tecDST_TAG_NEEDED). Tags are plaintext metadata, not encrypted.
capabilities.gotchas: Tags are NOT enforced by default — a payment without a DestinationTag to an exchange address often becomes unrecoverable (lost-to-support) unless the receiver set asfRequireDest. Tags are public plaintext, not private. They are arbitrary integers with no protocol-level meaning beyond the asfRequireDest gate — the mapping lives entirely in the receiver's off-ledger system. Always set asfRequireDest on shared/custodial receiving accounts to fail-closed on missing tags.

best_for.purpose: Routing deposits to exchange/custodial subaccounts
Enforcing tagged deposits via asfRequireDest
Mapping one game-treasury address to many players

sources.title: Source and Destination Tags (Common Fields)
sources.claim: SourceTag and DestinationTag are optional integers that identify a sender/recipient subaccount within a hosted address; asfRequireDest can force incoming payments to include a DestinationTag.
